business.concept.processes.subject: business_studies
business.concept.processes.oneLine: the systems a customer moves through to get the service: ordering, paying, waiting, collecting.
business.concept.processes.title: Processes in the marketing mix
business.concept.processes.quick: Processes are the systems a customer moves through to get the service: how an order is placed, paid for, prepared, handed over and fixed when it goes wrong. They are part of what the customer is buying, because for a service the experience of getting it cannot be separated from the thing itself.
readMore: A good or a service is bought through a sequence of steps, and for a service that sequence is visible to the customer. Choosing, queuing, ordering, paying, waiting, collecting and returning are all process steps. Some are done by staff, some by equipment such as a kiosk or an app, and some by the customer themselves. The marketing decision is which steps exist at all, who performs them, in what order, and how much time and effort each one costs the customer.

Processes are one of the three extra elements of the services marketing mix, alongside people and physical evidence. They are separated out because a service is intangible and is produced at the moment it is consumed, so the customer judges quality partly by how smoothly the delivery ran. A business can sell an identical product and lose to a competitor purely on the process around it.

A target market changes processes because different customers are prepared to spend different things. Some will spend time but not money, some will spend money to save time, some want to control the detail of what they receive, and some want no decisions at all. Once a business identifies which of these describes its target market, the process is redesigned to remove whatever that group is least willing to give up. That is why the customer expectation is the cause and the process change is the effect, and not the other way around.

Process changes are rarely free. Self service shifts work onto the customer and can suit one segment while alienating another. Extra choice at the ordering step slows the queue behind it. Faster collection can need more space, more staff at peak, or investment in equipment. A strong answer names the gain and is honest about what it costs.
confusions: Processes are not the product. Changing what is sold is a product strategy; changing how it is obtained is a process strategy.
Processes are not place. Place is where and through which channel the customer buys; processes are the sequence of steps once they are there.
Naming the technology is not analysis. An app or a kiosk is the means; the answer has to say which step it removed and for whom.
The cause runs from the customer to the business. A process did not change because the technology existed, it changed because a target market would not tolerate the old one.
business.concept.processes.example: A hardware shop finds its main customers are tradespeople who arrive before seven in the morning and cannot wait. It adds a phone-ahead order and a collection bay at the front of the store. Nothing about the products changed; the sequence the customer moves through did, and it changed because of who the customer is.
business.concept.processes.syllabusLabel: Marketing · marketing strategies · people, processes and physical evidence

business.concept.people.subject: business_studies
business.concept.people.oneLine: the staff a customer deals with, who are part of what a service customer is buying.
business.concept.people.title: People in the marketing mix
business.concept.people.quick: People are the staff who deliver a service. For a service the person and the product cannot be separated, so how staff behave, what they know and how consistent they are is part of what the customer pays for.
readMore: A service is produced at the moment it is consumed, and usually by a person. That makes the employee part of the offering rather than a cost behind it. Two businesses can sell the same thing and be judged differently entirely on who handed it over.

A target market changes people decisions because different customers want different things from the person serving them. Some want speed and no conversation. Some want advice and will wait for it. Some want the same experience in every store, which is a demand for consistency rather than for personality. The business responds by changing who it hires, what it trains them to do, and how tightly it standardises what they say and do.
confusions: People is not staffing levels alone. How many staff are on is part of it; what they are trained to do is the larger part.
People is not processes. Who serves the customer is people; the sequence of steps they are serving them through is processes.
business.concept.people.example: A garden centre serving hobby gardeners hires staff who can identify a plant from a photograph and will spend ten minutes doing it. A wholesale nursery serving landscapers hires staff who can load a truck quickly and say very little. Same product, opposite people decision, and the target market is the reason.
business.concept.people.syllabusLabel: Marketing · marketing strategies · people, processes and physical evidence

business.concept.training.subject: business_studies
business.concept.training.oneLine: teaching staff what to do and how to do it, so that what a customer receives does not depend on who is serving.
business.concept.training.title: Training
business.concept.training.quick: Training is how a business makes what its staff do predictable. It turns an intention about service into something that actually happens at every counter, on every shift, in every store.
readMore: Marketing decisions about people are delivered through training. A business can decide its target market wants unhurried advice, but that decision only reaches the customer if the staff know the range well enough to give it. Training is the mechanism between the marketing decision and the customer's experience.

The more a target market values consistency, the more tightly training is standardised. A customer who expects the same thing in every store is buying predictability, and predictability is produced by everyone being taught the same steps rather than by everyone being talented.
confusions: Training is not motivation. Teaching someone the steps and making them want to take them are different problems with different strategies.
Saying staff are trained proves nothing. The answer has to say what they were trained to do and which customer expectation that serves.
business.concept.training.example: A coffee chain whose customers expect the same drink in every city trains to a written recipe and times the shot. A single independent cafe whose customers come for the barista does not, because there nothing is meant to be identical.
business.concept.training.syllabusLabel: Marketing · marketing strategies · people, processes and physical evidence

business.concept.servicestandards.subject: business_studies
business.concept.servicestandards.oneLine: the level of service a business commits to, written down so it can be trained for and checked.
business.concept.servicestandards.title: Service standards
business.concept.servicestandards.quick: A service standard is the business stating what a customer will get: how long a wait should be, how a complaint is handled, what a staff member says. It is what turns a service intention into something that can be taught and measured.

business.concept.servicescape.subject: business_studies
business.concept.servicescape.oneLine: the formal name for the physical surroundings a service is delivered in.
business.concept.servicescape.title: Servicescape
business.concept.servicescape.quick: Business Studies sometimes calls the physical surroundings of a service the servicescape: the layout, lighting, seating, signage and general condition of the place the service happens in. Understand the surroundings first; the word is only the label for them.

business.concept.customerengagement.subject: business_studies
business.concept.customerengagement.oneLine: how far customers actually interact with a business rather than only seeing its marketing.
business.concept.customerengagement.title: Customer engagement
business.concept.customerengagement.quick: Engagement is the difference between a customer seeing something and doing something: opening the app, joining the loyalty scheme, leaving a review. It matters in e-marketing because a channel that reaches people without moving them is not doing the work.

business.lesson.mkt01-pe-service.subject: business_studies
business.lesson.mkt01-pe-service.know: A decision about staff only reaches the customer through what those staff are taught to do.
chain: customers judge the service on the person serving them
the business decides what good service is here
staff are trained to that standard
what the customer gets stops depending on who is on shift

misconception.head: Two of the elements are easy to swap

a.line: who serves the customer, and what they were taught to do.

b.line: the sequence of steps they are serving them through.

example.text: An optician whose customers come for the eye test trains every branch to the same twenty minute examination. The lenses are the same everywhere; the reason people return is the person.
example.pattern: the product did not change; what the staff were taught to do did

try.prompt: Customers say the advice they get depends on which branch they visit. Which change most directly addresses that?

options.text: Train every branch to the same service standard
Advertise the quality of the advice
options.repair: Advertising is promotion. It tells customers what to expect; it does not change what they actually get from the person in front of them.
When a customer can come is closer to place. This argument is about who serves them and what that person was taught.

try.onRight: Right. The inconsistency is in what staff were taught, so the fix is in training rather than in anything the customer can see.

exploreRef.label: Read more about people in the marketing mix

business.lesson.mkt01-pr-convenience.subject: business_studies
business.lesson.mkt01-pr-convenience.know: Changing a process changes what the customer has to do, not what they are buying.
chain: less time and effort to buy

misconception.head: Two of the elements are easy to swap

a.line: the systems a customer moves through to buy.

b.line: the staff who serve them while they do.

example.text: A cinema that lets you choose your seat in the app has changed a process. The film is exactly the same.
example.pattern: the thing being sold did not change; what the customer had to do to get it did

try.prompt: Customers say ordering takes too long. Which change most directly addresses that?

options.text: Let customers order and pay in the app

options.repair: Advertising changes promotion, not what a customer has to do to buy. Look again at ordering, payment or collection.

options.text: Redesign the store so it looks smarter
options.repair: How the place looks is physical evidence. This argument is about what the customer has to DO.

try.onRight: Right. Ordering is a step the customer moves through, so changing it changes the process.

business.lesson.mkt01-pr-speed.subject: business_studies
business.lesson.mkt01-pr-speed.know: A process runs in steps, and some wait for the one before while others can run alongside. Cutting a wait usually means moving a step, not asking anyone to work harder.
chain: customers count waiting as a cost
steps are separated or run side by side
the queue moves whether or not the order is ready
the wait falls, especially at peak

misconception.head: Two answers that sound the same and are not

a.line: the same steps, done more quickly. That is a people point.

b.line: the queue no longer waits for it. That is a process point.

example.text: An airport that takes bags at a kerbside desk has moved a step out of the terminal queue. Nobody is walking any faster.
example.pattern: the wait fell because a step left the queue, not because anyone sped up

try.prompt: A queue builds because every order is only started once it has been taken. Which change most directly cuts the wait?

options.text: Start the most common orders before they are ordered

options.repair: Who serves the customer is a people point. This argument is about where a step sits in the process.

options.text: Put up a sign apologising for the wait
options.repair: That changes what the customer sees while waiting, not how long they wait. Look at the order of the steps.

try.onRight: Right. The step that caused the wait now happens before the queue reaches it.

business.lesson.mkt01-pr-customisation.subject: business_studies
business.lesson.mkt01-pr-customisation.know: A process built for identical orders breaks as soon as orders differ. Carrying a variation means capturing it once and holding it through every step that follows.
chain: customers expect to change the order
the ordering system captures the variation
the right order arrives without a correction

misconception.head: Two arguments that look alike and are not

a.line: what is on offer. That is a product point.

b.line: whether the variation survives the process. That is this argument.

example.text: A paint shop that mixes to a code the customer chose has a process built for variation. The product is still paint.
example.pattern: the range did not widen; the process learned to carry a change

try.prompt: Customers keep receiving a different version of what they asked for. Which change most directly addresses that?

options.text: Let customers enter the change themselves when they order
Add more items to the menu
options.repair: More choice is a product point. The problem here is whether a change survives the process.

options.text: Train staff to apologise more quickly
options.repair: That is what happens after the error. This argument is about the step where the change is captured.

try.onRight: Right. Captured by the customer at the start, the variation does not have to survive being passed on.

mcdonalds.operations.standardised-produc.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.standardised-produc.label: Standardised production system
mcdonalds.operations.standardised-produc.fact: McDonald's builds its core menu items to the same specifications, portion sizes and cooking times wherever they are sold, using a standardised process, although some equipment and part of the menu vary from market to market. Making identical items in very high volume lowers the cost of each unit, because the cost of equipment, product design and training is spread over an enormous number of sales.
mcdonalds.operations.standardised-produc.use: Use for the strategic role of operations management: link standardisation and high volume to a lower cost per unit, then state that operations is what makes a cost leadership strategy possible. Concede that the menu is not identical everywhere, which shows the limit of standardisation.

mcdonalds.operations.interdependence-at-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.interdependence-at-.label: Interdependence at a menu launch
mcdonalds.operations.interdependence-at-.fact: When McDonald's adds an item to the menu, marketing plans the promotion and forecasts demand, operations changes kitchen procedures and orders the new ingredients, human resources retrains crew to make it inside the same service time, and finance approves the spending on equipment and stock. If one function is not ready, the item is slow, inconsistent or unavailable and the promotion is wasted.
mcdonalds.operations.interdependence-at-.use: Use for interdependence with other key business functions: take marketing, human resources and finance in turn, say what each supplies to operations, then argue that a new product cannot reach the customer unless all four functions move together.

mcdonalds.operations.a-good-and-a-servic.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.a-good-and-a-servic.label: A good and a service in one transaction
mcdonalds.operations.a-good-and-a-servic.fact: A McDonald's meal is a good, a tangible item the customer takes and consumes, but ordering at a counter, kiosk, drive through window or delivery app, the seating and cleaning, and the speed of service are services, produced and consumed on the spot and impossible to store. Operations therefore runs a production process, like a manufacturer, and a customer contact process, like a service business, in the same building at the same time.
mcdonalds.operations.a-good-and-a-servic.use: Use for goods and/or services in different industries: show that fast food sits between manufacturing and pure service, then contrast it with an industry at each end, car manufacturing where goods are stored and inspected before sale, and accounting where the output is intangible and customised.

mcdonalds.operations.global-menu-localis.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.global-menu-localis.label: Global menu localisation
mcdonalds.operations.global-menu-localis.fact: McDonald's runs restaurants in many countries and keeps its core products and production system the same everywhere, but changes part of the menu to suit local tastes, religious requirements and locally available ingredients. Globalisation therefore pushes operations two ways at once, towards standardisation for cost and towards localisation for acceptance.
mcdonalds.operations.global-menu-localis.use: Use for globalisation as an influence: show the tension between standardising the process to cut cost and adapting the menu so the product is accepted in each market, then judge which matters more for a business competing on price.

mcdonalds.operations.packaging-waste-the.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.packaging-waste-the.label: Packaging waste, the law and voluntary action
mcdonalds.operations.packaging-waste-the.fact: Fast food is served in single use packaging, so McDonald's faces constant pressure over waste. In New South Wales, single use plastic straws, stirrers, cutlery, plates, bowls without lids and expanded polystyrene foodware and cups are banned by law, as are lightweight plastic shopping bags, so removing those items is legal compliance and the minimum standard, not a choice. Food safety and labelling law is legal compliance too. Voluntary steps that no law requires are the ethical responsibility side: moving remaining packaging to recyclable or fibre based materials, sourcing certified fibre for cups and boxes, separating waste for recycling inside the restaurant, and donating surplus food.
mcdonalds.operations.packaging-waste-the.use: Use for corporate social responsibility: put the banned plastic items on the legal compliance side and the voluntary packaging and waste choices on the ethical responsibility side. Then split the impact, packaging and waste as environmental sustainability and donated food and safe workplaces as social responsibility. Never call an action ethical if the law already requires it.

mcdonalds.operations.inputs-transformed-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.inputs-transformed-.label: Inputs, transformed and transforming
mcdonalds.operations.inputs-transformed-.fact: At McDonald's the transformed resources are materials such as beef patties, buns, potatoes and drink syrup, information such as the order entered at the counter, kiosk or app, and the customers themselves, who move through the queue and are served. The transforming resources are the crew and their training, and the facilities, meaning the restaurant, the kitchen equipment and the drive through lane.
mcdonalds.operations.inputs-transformed-.use: Use for inputs: name materials, information and customers as the three transformed resources, then human resources and facilities as transforming, so each category is proved with a concrete example rather than defined in the abstract.

mcdonalds.operations.volume-variety-vari.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.volume-variety-vari.label: Volume, variety, variation and visibility
mcdonalds.operations.volume-variety-vari.fact: McDonald's is high volume, making a small number of items over and over. Its variety is narrow compared with a full service restaurant, although kiosks and the app let a customer add or remove ingredients, which lifts variety slightly and is an example of customisation. Demand varies sharply across the day around meal time peaks, so rosters and stock are planned around them. Visibility is split: front of house at the counter, kiosk, drive through window and seating area, customer contact is high, so waiting time, order accuracy and staff presentation are on show, while most food production happens back of house out of sight, which is exactly why it can be standardised for speed.
mcdonalds.operations.volume-variety-vari.use: Use for the influence of volume, variety, variation in demand and visibility: give one example for each of the four, and split visibility into front of house and back of house, because that split explains why the process can be engineered for speed while the service still has to look right.

mcdonalds.operations.technology-task-des.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.technology-task-des.label: Technology, task design and process layout
mcdonalds.operations.technology-task-des.fact: The kitchen is laid out as an assembly line, and each crew member is given a narrow, repeated task such as the fryer, the grill or assembly, which is specific task design. Technology supports the layout: self service ordering kiosks, app and delivery orders, and kitchen screens that display each order to the crew member who has to make it.
mcdonalds.operations.technology-task-des.use: Use for technology, task design and process layout: explain that narrow task design plus a product layout raises speed and consistency, and that kiosks shift order taking to the customer, freeing crew for production and service.

mcdonalds.operations.outputs-order-accur.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.outputs-order-accur.label: Outputs, order accuracy and service time
mcdonalds.operations.outputs-order-accur.fact: What a McDonald's customer judges is the meal plus the service around it: whether the order is correct, hot and fast. Order accuracy is checked at handover and the standard response to a wrong order is to remake it or refund it. Service times, especially at the drive through, are measured, and app and delivery orders can be tracked by the customer. Food carries no repair warranty, because it is consumed immediately, so the equivalent output promise is the remake or refund, sitting on top of the consumer guarantees every buyer has under Australian Consumer Law.
mcdonalds.operations.outputs-order-accur.use: Use for outputs: give customer service examples first, then handle warranties honestly by explaining that a food business relies on a remake or refund and on consumer guarantees rather than a repair warranty, and finish by feeding complaint and remake data back into monitoring, control and improvement.

mcdonalds.operations.approved-suppliers-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.approved-suppliers-.label: Approved suppliers and distribution centres
mcdonalds.operations.approved-suppliers-.fact: McDonald's buys from a small group of approved suppliers on long term contracts and moves stock through distribution centres that deliver to restaurants on a set schedule. Suppliers must meet set product specifications, so a patty or a bun is the same in every restaurant they supply. In Australia the business states that the large majority of its food inputs, including beef, potatoes, chicken, dairy and bakery items, comes from Australian farmers and suppliers, which protects freshness and country of origin, while global sourcing applies more to non food inputs such as equipment and packaging and to markets that have no local supply.
mcdonalds.operations.approved-suppliers-.use: Use for supply chain management: connect the distribution centre schedule to logistics and the supplier specifications to the quality and dependability performance objectives. Do not argue that the Australian business sources its food globally, and keep bulk buying power for the global factors card under economies of scale.

mcdonalds.operations.frozen-stock-fifo-a.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.frozen-stock-fifo-a.label: Frozen stock, FIFO and made to order
mcdonalds.operations.frozen-stock-fifo-a.fact: McDonald's splits its inputs. Frozen inputs such as patties and fries arrive on a set delivery schedule and are held in freezers, so their shelf life is long and the restaurant carries a buffer between deliveries. Fresh and chilled inputs such as lettuce, tomato, dairy and buns have a short shelf life, so they are rotated first in first out, oldest used first, with set holding times. Just in time sits at the other end of the process: most items are cooked or assembled after the order is placed, so finished goods inventory is close to zero and little prepared food is thrown away.
mcdonalds.operations.frozen-stock-fifo-a.use: Use for inventory management: put FIFO on the fresh and chilled inputs and just in time on the finished product rather than on the deliveries. Then give the disadvantage, that with almost no finished stock a delivery failure or an equipment breakdown takes an item off sale straight away.

mcdonalds.operations.quality-control-ass.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.quality-control-ass.label: Quality control, assurance and improvement
mcdonalds.operations.quality-control-ass.fact: Quality control at McDonald's is checking during and after production, for example cooking times, food temperatures and holding times before food is served. Quality assurance is the set standards and procedures every restaurant must follow, including franchised restaurants, checked by audit. Quality improvement comes from crew training, acting on customer feedback and changing procedures when a fault keeps recurring.
mcdonalds.operations.quality-control-ass.use: Use for quality management: give one example under control, one under assurance and one under improvement, then judge that assurance is what makes the same standard possible across restaurants the company does not operate itself.

mcdonalds.operations.performance-objecti.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.performance-objecti.label: Performance objectives on the restaurant floor
mcdonalds.operations.performance-objecti.fact: Every performance objective is visible in a McDonald's restaurant. Speed: counter and drive through service times are measured and the process is built around them. Dependability: the same core item is meant to look and taste the same on every visit and in every restaurant. Flexibility: the line switches from the breakfast menu to the main menu and staffing rises and falls with meal time peaks. Customisation: kiosks and the app let a customer add or remove ingredients. Quality: cooking temperatures and holding times govern what may be served. Cost: standardised items in high volume hold the cost per unit down.
mcdonalds.operations.performance-objecti.use: Use for performance objectives: give one example for each of the six, then judge the trade off, that customisation through kiosks and the app slows the line and raises cost, which is one reason the core menu stays narrow.

mcdonalds.operations.kiosks-and-the-app-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.kiosks-and-the-app-.label: Kiosks and the app beside the grill
mcdonalds.operations.kiosks-and-the-app-.fact: Newer technology runs alongside long established equipment in a McDonald's restaurant. Ordering kiosks, the mobile app, delivery platform integration and kitchen display screens are the newer layer, shifting order taking to the customer and routing orders automatically. Grills, fryers, freezers and holding cabinets are established technology, proven, familiar to crew and cheaper to buy, maintain and staff. As kiosks and apps spread across the industry they stop being an advantage and become established themselves.
mcdonalds.operations.kiosks-and-the-app-.use: Use for technology, leading edge and established: name one of each inside the same business, then assess the trade off, that newer technology can raise speed and customisation but costs capital and retraining, while established equipment is reliable and cheap yet gives no advantage over rivals with the same gear.

mcdonalds.operations.outsourcing-and-why.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.outsourcing-and-why.label: Outsourcing, and why franchising is not outsourcing
mcdonalds.operations.outsourcing-and-why.fact: Support functions around a McDonald's restaurant are commonly contracted to outside providers instead of being done in house, for example equipment maintenance, waste removal, cleaning and construction, and delivery to the customer is carried out through third party delivery platforms. Franchising is not outsourcing: a franchisee is an independent operator who runs a whole restaurant under licence, paying fees and following the franchisor's system, rather than a contractor performing one function on the business's behalf.
mcdonalds.operations.outsourcing-and-why.use: Use for outsourcing: name the function contracted out, then argue both sides, specialist expertise and lower fixed cost against loss of direct control over quality and the margin paid to a delivery platform. Add the franchising caution to show you know what outsourcing actually means.

mcdonalds.operations.resistance-when-kio.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.resistance-when-kio.label: Resistance when kiosks and table service arrived
mcdonalds.operations.resistance-when-kio.fact: Bringing ordering kiosks, table service and delivery into restaurants changed how crew work and cost money before any benefit arrived. Restaurants had to be refitted and equipment bought, which is a financial cost, and crew and franchisees had to be retrained into new roles such as carrying food to tables and managing delivery orders. Inertia is the other barrier, because staff who are fast and confident on the old counter routine can resist a system that makes them slower until they learn it.
mcdonalds.operations.resistance-when-kio.use: Use for overcoming resistance to change: separate the financial cost of refitting and retraining from the inertia of people used to the old routine, then name the strategies, consulting staff early, retraining before the changeover and rolling the change out restaurant by restaurant so problems are found cheaply.

mcdonalds.operations.global-scale-menu-t.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.operations.global-scale-menu-t.label: Global scale, menu trials and test kitchens
mcdonalds.operations.global-scale-menu-t.fact: Operating in many countries gives McDonald's each of the global factors. Global sourcing: equipment, packaging and inputs that are not available locally can be bought from suppliers in other countries. Economies of scale: buying ingredients, packaging and equipment for a very large number of restaurants spreads fixed costs and gives buying power, lowering the cost per unit. Scanning and learning: an item or service idea that works in one country is studied and rolled out to others, and several well known menu items began in a single market. Research and development: new products and processes are developed and tested in product development kitchens before they reach restaurants.
mcdonalds.operations.global-scale-menu-t.use: Use for global factors: give one example under each of the four. Put bulk buying power under economies of scale rather than calling it global sourcing, and use the menu trial as scanning and learning that lowers the risk of a national rollout.

mcdonalds.marketing.golden-arches-global.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.golden-arches-global.label: Golden Arches global branding
mcdonalds.marketing.golden-arches-global.fact: McDonald's uses the same Golden Arches logo and red and yellow colour scheme in almost every market, so customers recognise the brand without reading any words. Core products such as the Big Mac are sold under the same name in most markets, although the name and recipe change where local tastes or laws require it. The brand covers both a good, the food, and a service, the ordering and dining experience.
mcdonalds.marketing.golden-arches-global.use: Use for the strategic role of marketing: strong global branding builds market share and customer loyalty, which is how marketing contributes to McDonald's overall business objectives of profit and growth.

mcdonalds.marketing.economic-and-sociocu.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.economic-and-sociocu.label: Economic and sociocultural influences on customer choice
mcdonalds.marketing.economic-and-sociocu.fact: Customer choice at McDonald's is shaped by economic conditions, because a low priced value range attracts customers when household budgets tighten, and by sociocultural change, because rising interest in healthier eating pushed McDonald's to change its range over time, adding items such as grilled chicken, fruit, water and milk options and lower kilojoule choices, and to trial plant based burgers in some markets. Some of these items have since been changed or withdrawn where they did not sell.
mcdonalds.marketing.economic-and-sociocu.use: Use for factors influencing customer choice: name the economic factor and the sociocultural factor, then link back by saying McDonald's changed what it offers because customer preferences changed.

mcdonalds.marketing.kilojoule-labelling-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.kilojoule-labelling-.label: Kilojoule labelling and advertising to children
mcdonalds.marketing.kilojoule-labelling-.fact: Large fast food chains including McDonald's must display kilojoule information on menu boards in New South Wales, which is legal compliance with a government influence. Advertising to children, especially the toy in the Happy Meal, is a long running ethical criticism of McDonald's, and it has responded over time by changing what a Happy Meal can contain, for example offering water and milk as drink choices rather than only soft drink.
mcdonalds.marketing.kilojoule-labelling-.use: Use for government influence and for ethical marketing: show McDonald's meets the legal requirement on kilojoule display, then goes beyond legal compliance by changing Happy Meal choices in response to public criticism.

mcdonalds.marketing.consumer-law-and-adv.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.consumer-law-and-adv.label: Consumer law and advertising claims
mcdonalds.marketing.consumer-law-and-adv.fact: McDonald's advertising is governed by the Australian Consumer Law, which prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct, so promotional images and claims about ingredients, portion sizes and prices must match what the customer actually receives, and an advertised price must be honoured at the counter. Implied conditions also apply to every sale, so the food must be of acceptable quality and fit to eat, and the business cannot advertise its way out of them.
mcdonalds.marketing.consumer-law-and-adv.use: Use for consumer laws: name deceptive and misleading advertising, apply it by saying a McDonald's promotional image and advertised price must match what is actually served and charged, then explain that breaching it risks penalties and lasting damage to a brand built on trust.

mcdonalds.marketing.big-mac-in-the-matur.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.big-mac-in-the-matur.label: Big Mac in the maturity stage
mcdonalds.marketing.big-mac-in-the-matur.fact: Core McDonald's products such as the Big Mac, the Quarter Pounder and fries have been sold for decades, so they are usually classified as sitting in the maturity stage of the product life cycle, where sales are steady rather than growing quickly and competition is strong. McDonald's applies extension strategies to that stage, using limited time offers, promotional tie ins, restyled menus and separate ranges such as McCafe.
mcdonalds.marketing.big-mac-in-the-matur.use: Use in situational analysis: identify the maturity stage, then name an extension strategy such as a limited time offer, so you link the product life cycle tool to an actual strategy instead of just labelling the stage.

mcdonalds.marketing.test-restaurants-and.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.test-restaurants-and.label: Test restaurants and customer feedback surveys
mcdonalds.marketing.test-restaurants-and.fact: McDonald's researches customers before a national launch: new menu items are commonly trialled in a limited number of restaurants or in one region first, and customers are invited to give feedback through surveys, often reached by a code printed on the receipt or through the app.
mcdonalds.marketing.test-restaurants-and.use: Use for market research and for implementation, monitoring and controlling: trialling in test restaurants is primary data collection, and it lets McDonald's compare actual results with planned results before it revises or scales the strategy.

mcdonalds.marketing.segments-served-by-h.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.segments-served-by-h.label: Segments served by Happy Meal and McCafe
mcdonalds.marketing.segments-served-by-h.fact: McDonald's sells to a mass market but still segments it. Happy Meals with a toy target families with young children, McCafe targets coffee drinkers who might otherwise choose a cafe, and extended or twenty four hour trading at selected restaurants targets shift workers and students.
mcdonalds.marketing.segments-served-by-h.use: Use for market segmentation, differentiation and positioning: name the segment, name the product built for it, then argue that product differentiation lets one brand serve several segments at once without losing its overall position.

mcdonalds.marketing.promotion-mix-from-a.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.promotion-mix-from-a.label: Promotion mix from advertising to sponsorship
mcdonalds.marketing.promotion-mix-from-a.fact: McDonald's uses the full promotion mix: advertising on television, outdoor billboards and social media; sales promotions such as app only vouchers, limited time offers and collectable promotions; publicity and public relations through community and junior sport sponsorship and its long association with Ronald McDonald House Charities; and relationship marketing through the rewards scheme in its app.
mcdonalds.marketing.promotion-mix-from-a.use: Use for promotion: name one element of the promotion mix, name the McDonald's example, then explain its purpose, for example that app only vouchers both drive repeat visits and show the business which offers actually worked.

mcdonalds.marketing.price-points-from-va.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.price-points-from-va.label: Price points from value range to McCafe
mcdonalds.marketing.price-points-from-va.fact: McDonald's uses clear price points: a value range priced well below a full meal, a standard menu, and premium ranges such as McCafe. The low price points are designed to bring high customer numbers through the door, and customers are then encouraged to add fries, a drink or a dessert, so total sales per customer rise even though the entry item is cheap.
mcdonalds.marketing.price-points-from-va.use: Use for pricing strategies: name price points rather than loss leaders, then explain that cheap entry price levels lift customer numbers and average spend per visit, while the premium range works through price and quality interaction.

mcdonalds.marketing.intensive-distributi.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.intensive-distributi.label: Intensive distribution and standardised service
mcdonalds.marketing.intensive-distributi.fact: McDonald's distributes intensively through a large network of company owned and franchised restaurants, drive through lanes, delivery through third party platforms, and self service ordering kiosks. Standardised crew uniforms, signage, packaging and menu boards, plus a familiar counter, kiosk and drive through layout, act as physical evidence that the service will feel the same wherever the customer goes.
mcdonalds.marketing.intensive-distributi.use: Use for place and distribution and for people, processes and physical evidence: argue that convenience and consistency are the benefits, which supports positioning McDonald's as fast, reliable and familiar.

mcdonalds.marketing.standardisation-with.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.standardisation-with.label: Standardisation with local customisation
mcdonalds.marketing.standardisation-with.fact: McDonald's standardises its core menu and branding worldwide, then customises for local markets. Restaurants in India serve no beef and offer chicken and vegetarian burgers instead, and other markets add items suited to local tastes, such as rice based or teriyaki based products in parts of Asia.
mcdonalds.marketing.standardisation-with.use: Use for global marketing: state that McDonald's blends standardisation, which gives economies of scale, with customisation, which answers sociocultural and legal difference, so a global brand keeps local relevance.

mcdonalds.marketing.app-loyalty-rewards-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.marketing.app-loyalty-rewards-.label: App, loyalty rewards and mobile ordering
mcdonalds.marketing.app-loyalty-rewards-.fact: McDonald's runs e-marketing through its mobile app, which carries digital vouchers, a loyalty rewards scheme, mobile ordering and payment, and a restaurant locator. It also promotes through social media pages and reaches customers at home through third party delivery platforms.
mcdonalds.marketing.app-loyalty-rewards-.use: Use for e-marketing: explain that the app collects customer data and pushes targeted offers, which raises repeat purchase and lets McDonald's monitor which promotions actually work.

mcdonalds.finance.franchising-funds-netw.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.franchising-funds-netw.label: Franchising funds network growth
mcdonalds.finance.franchising-funds-netw.fact: Most McDonald's restaurants worldwide are operated by franchisees rather than by the company itself. McDonald's typically secures and develops the site and building, while the franchisee funds much of the equipment, fit-out and running costs and pays McDonald's ongoing fees plus rent. The network therefore grows without the company funding every new restaurant out of its own retained profits or borrowings.
mcdonalds.finance.franchising-funds-netw.use: Use for the objective of growth: explain that franchisee capital pays for a large part of each new restaurant, so financial management supports long-term growth of the network without the business having to raise the full cost of every site itself. Do not claim this keeps its gearing low.

mcdonalds.finance.finance-funds-every-ot.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.finance-funds-every-ot.label: Finance funds every other function
mcdonalds.finance.finance-funds-every-ot.fact: Finance sets and controls the budget that every other function spends. Marketing needs funds approved for advertising and value menu promotions, operations needs capital for self-order kiosks, drive-through upgrades and delivery, and human resources needs money for crew wages and training. No plan proceeds unless finance can supply the funds and monitor how they are spent.
mcdonalds.finance.finance-funds-every-ot.use: Name one concrete spend, such as kiosks or a value menu campaign, then explain that finance allocates and monitors those funds while the sales those spends generate become the revenue finance reports, proving the key business functions are interdependent rather than working in isolation.

mcdonalds.finance.listed-parent-using-re.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.listed-parent-using-re.label: Listed parent using retained profits and borrowing
mcdonalds.finance.listed-parent-using-re.fact: McDonald's Corporation is a listed public company whose ordinary shares trade on a stock exchange in the United States, and the Australian business sits inside that global group. It funds itself mainly from retained profits and from borrowing in capital markets, and it returns cash to shareholders as dividends.
mcdonalds.finance.listed-parent-using-re.use: Use to compare internal and external finance as this business actually uses them: retained profits cost nothing to raise and keep control, while debt brings cash in quickly and the interest is tax deductible, but it must be repaid with interest whatever the profit. Treat new issues, rights issues, placements and share purchase plans as equity options open to any listed company, not as this business's practice.

mcdonalds.finance.australian-company-und.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.australian-company-und.label: Australian company under ASIC and company tax
mcdonalds.finance.australian-company-und.fact: The Australian business operates as a company under the Corporations Act, so it is subject to Australian Securities and Investments Commission oversight of company registration, financial reporting and disclosure, and it pays Australian company tax on its taxable profits, which reduces the funds left to retain in the business. Its parent company is listed on a stock exchange in the United States, not on the Australian Securities Exchange.
mcdonalds.finance.australian-company-und.use: Use for influence of government: one point on the Australian Securities and Investments Commission enforcing the Corporations Act and reporting and disclosure requirements, and one point on company tax as a budgeted cash outflow that reduces retained profits. Do not write that this business raises equity on the Australian Securities Exchange.

mcdonalds.finance.interest-rates-oversea.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.interest-rates-oversea.label: Interest rates, overseas funds and the economic outlook
mcdonalds.finance.interest-rates-oversea.fact: McDonald's typically secures and develops the site and building while the franchisee funds much of the equipment, fit-out and running costs, so both parties borrow to build, fit out or refurbish and both are exposed to interest rates. As a multinational, the group can also raise funds in overseas capital markets, where interest rates and the availability of funds differ from Australia, although borrowing abroad adds exchange rate risk on repayments. On the economic outlook, value pricing can attract customers trading down from more expensive options, but a weaker economy can also reduce the total number of visits.
mcdonalds.finance.interest-rates-oversea.use: Use for global market influences and cover all three named influences: higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and can slow expansion; availability of funds and rates differ between countries, so a multinational can borrow where funds are cheaper and easier to obtain, at the price of currency risk; and argue the economic outlook both ways rather than assuming value pricing protects revenue.

mcdonalds.finance.immediate-cash-sales-a.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.immediate-cash-sales-a.label: Immediate cash sales, almost no customer receivables
mcdonalds.finance.immediate-cash-sales-a.fact: Customers pay at the counter, kiosk, drive-through or app at the moment they buy, so restaurants collect cash immediately and carry almost no customer receivables, while supplier invoices are paid later on agreed credit terms. This timing gap gives the business a steady inflow of cash to meet short-term debts.
mcdonalds.finance.immediate-cash-sales-a.use: Use in cash flow or liquidity answers: explain that immediate cash sales with delayed supplier payments strengthen operating activities in the cash flow statement, so a current ratio below the usual benchmark is not automatically a liquidity problem for this kind of business.

mcdonalds.finance.two-levels-of-margin-r.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.two-levels-of-margin-r.label: Two levels of margin, restaurant and corporation
mcdonalds.finance.two-levels-of-margin-r.fact: At restaurant level each item sold earns only a small margin, so restaurant profitability depends on high volume and on tight control of food, wage and occupancy costs, which is what the expense ratio measures. The corporation's own revenue is different: it comes mainly from franchise fees and rent paid by franchisees, which carry much higher margins than operating a restaurant.
mcdonalds.finance.two-levels-of-margin-r.use: Use for financial ratios, but say which entity you are analysing first. For a restaurant, argue that a small rise in the expense ratio cuts net profit sharply because the margin per item is thin. For the corporation, note that fee and rent revenue supports a much stronger net profit ratio. Then compare over different time periods and with similar quick service chains.

mcdonalds.finance.choosing-debt-or-equit.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.choosing-debt-or-equit.label: Choosing debt or equity for expansion
mcdonalds.finance.choosing-debt-or-equit.fact: A large listed group such as McDonald's funds expansion mainly from retained profits and borrowing rather than by issuing new shares, while a franchisee opening a restaurant usually combines their own funds with a bank loan or a lease over equipment. Interest on borrowings is a tax deductible expense, but principal and interest must be repaid whether or not the restaurant trades well.
mcdonalds.finance.choosing-debt-or-equit.use: Use for planning and implementing: judge debt against equity for a stated purpose. Debt is faster to arrange, keeps ownership with existing owners and its interest is tax deductible, but it raises gearing and locks in fixed repayments; equity has no repayment obligation but dilutes ownership and shares future profits. Finish by matching the term of finance to the purpose, such as a lease or long-term loan for a fit-out and an overdraft only for a short-term cash gap.

mcdonalds.finance.consolidated-global-re.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.consolidated-global-re.label: Consolidated global reports and one-off gains
mcdonalds.finance.consolidated-global-re.fact: McDonald's reports consolidated results for a global group in United States dollars, so one set of statements hides how individual countries performed and is affected by exchange rate movements. Selling company operated restaurants to franchisees can also create one-off gains, which is why normalised earnings matter when judging trading performance.
mcdonalds.finance.consolidated-global-re.use: Use for limitations of financial reports: name normalised earnings and timing issues, explain that one-off gains from selling restaurants flatter the income statement, and add that the notes to the financial statements must be read to see the accounting methods behind the figures.

mcdonalds.finance.audited-accounts-and-d.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.audited-accounts-and-d.label: Audited accounts and disclosure in a listed group
mcdonalds.finance.audited-accounts-and-d.fact: As a listed public company the group prepares its financial statements under accounting standards, has them independently audited and publishes them for shareholders, and the Australian company must meet Corporations Act reporting and disclosure requirements. Ethical reporting means those statements are honest and complete, not merely technically legal, because franchisees, lenders, shareholders and employees all rely on them.
mcdonalds.finance.audited-accounts-and-d.use: Use for ethical issues related to financial reports: argue that independent audit and disclosure are the safeguards against window dressing, understated expenses or hidden debt, and separate legal compliance, meeting the reporting rules, from ethical responsibility, giving a true and fair view that does not mislead. Do not allege any specific wrongdoing by the business.

mcdonalds.finance.standardisation-as-cos.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.standardisation-as-cos.label: Standardisation as cost control, marketing as revenue control
mcdonalds.finance.standardisation-as-cos.fact: Cost control comes from standardisation: standardised equipment and set procedures across restaurants, with the menu adapted to local markets, plus bulk purchasing through long-term supplier agreements, which cuts cost per unit. Revenue control comes from marketing objectives such as value menu deals, app only offers, McCafe and delivery, all designed to lift sales.
mcdonalds.finance.standardisation-as-cos.use: Use for profitability management: pair a cost control, bulk purchasing and standardised procedures, with a revenue control, a value menu deal or app offer, then judge which contributed more to net profit. Note that the menu is adapted to local markets, so standardisation is not absolute.

mcdonalds.finance.property-leasing-and-w.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.property-leasing-and-w.label: Property, leasing and working capital
mcdonalds.finance.property-leasing-and-w.fact: McDonald's secures restaurant sites by buying property or taking long leases, then sub-leases many of those sites to franchisees, so rent is a major and reliable revenue stream and the business generally keeps those property interests rather than selling them. Leasing sites and equipment rather than buying them outright preserves cash and keeps working capital available for daily operations.
mcdonalds.finance.property-leasing-and-w.use: Use for working capital strategies: explain that leasing avoids a large upfront outlay so cash stays available for daily operations. Present sale and lease back separately, as a general strategy other businesses use to release cash tied up in property, not as something this business does, since it holds property in order to earn rent.

mcdonalds.finance.exchange-rate-exposure.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.finance.exchange-rate-exposure.label: Exchange rate exposure and hedging
mcdonalds.finance.exchange-rate-exposure.fact: McDonald's earns revenue in many different currencies and converts it back to United States dollars for reporting, so a stronger US dollar reduces the reported value of overseas earnings. Multinationals in this position manage the risk with hedging tools such as forward exchange contracts and by borrowing in local currencies so that revenue and repayments are in the same currency.
mcdonalds.finance.exchange-rate-exposure.use: Use for global financial management: identify exchange rate risk on overseas earnings, then evaluate hedging, saying it gives certainty for planning and budgeting although it costs money and gives up any gain from a favourable currency move.

mcdonalds.hr.franchise-model-splits-hr-r.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.franchise-model-splits-hr-r.label: Franchise model splits HR responsibility
mcdonalds.hr.franchise-model-splits-hr-r.fact: Most McDonald's restaurants are run by franchisees rather than by the company itself. The franchisee is the legal employer of the crew in that store, so recruitment, rostering, training delivery and discipline happen locally, while McDonald's corporate sets the operating standards, training systems and brand requirements the franchisee must follow.
mcdonalds.hr.franchise-model-splits-hr-r.use: Use for the strategic role of human resources and interdependence: it shows human resource management must deliver a consistent customer experience across independently owned stores, so tie it back to the word strategic in the question.

mcdonalds.hr.outsourcing-and-use-of-cont.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.outsourcing-and-use-of-cont.label: Outsourcing and use of contractors
mcdonalds.hr.outsourcing-and-use-of-cont.fact: McDonald's does not employ everyone who works around the business. Cleaning, maintenance, building work and equipment servicing are commonly done by contractors, and home delivery runs through third party delivery platforms whose riders are not McDonald's employees. Support functions such as payroll processing and online recruitment systems can also sit with external providers.
mcdonalds.hr.outsourcing-and-use-of-cont.use: Use for the outsourcing dot point, including domestic and global contractors: argue it lowers labour costs and lets human resource staff focus on crew, then weigh the loss of direct control over service quality.

mcdonalds.hr.national-employment-standar.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.national-employment-standar.label: National Employment Standards and the award set the floor
mcdonalds.hr.national-employment-standar.fact: In Australia, McDonald's crew are covered by the fast food industry award, which sits on top of the National Employment Standards. The award sets minimum wage rates, junior rates for younger workers, breaks and penalty rates, while the National Employment Standards set entitlements such as leave and notice of termination. Most crew are hired as casual or part time employees.
mcdonalds.hr.national-employment-standar.use: Use for the legal influence and the employment contract: argue human resource decisions on pay and rostering are constrained, not free, then judge how well the business complies. Treat enterprise agreements as a general option in the legal framework rather than as this business's current instrument.

mcdonalds.hr.work-health-and-safety-in-t.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.work-health-and-safety-in-t.label: Work health and safety in the restaurant
mcdonalds.hr.work-health-and-safety-in-t.fact: A McDonald's kitchen contains hot fryers, grills, wet floors, sharp equipment and cleaning chemicals, so work health and safety is a genuine human resource issue. The response is standardised safety procedures, compulsory safety training during induction, protective equipment, slip resistant flooring and incident reporting, supported by workers compensation cover for injured staff.
mcdonalds.hr.work-health-and-safety-in-t.use: Use for work health and safety and workers compensation, and again for the accidents indicator: link compulsory safety training to fewer accidents, lower workers compensation premiums and less lost time.

mcdonalds.hr.technology-and-changing-wor.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.technology-and-changing-wor.label: Technology and changing work patterns
mcdonalds.hr.technology-and-changing-wor.fact: Self service ordering kiosks, mobile app ordering and delivery platforms have changed what crew actually do, shifting labour away from taking orders at the counter towards assembling and dispatching orders. McDonald's also rosters a largely casual and part time workforce, much of it students, around school, study and family commitments.
mcdonalds.hr.technology-and-changing-wor.use: Use for technological and social influences: argue technology redesigned jobs and forced retraining, and that flexible rostering answers changing work patterns and casualisation. Name the influence the question asks about in your topic sentence.

mcdonalds.hr.standardised-acquisition-an.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.standardised-acquisition-an.label: Standardised acquisition and development
mcdonalds.hr.standardised-acquisition-an.fact: New crew apply online or in store, then move through a standardised induction and structured on the job training, learning one station at a time such as grill, fries, front counter or drive through, using set procedures and e-learning modules. Managers are developed further through the company's own structured management training programs, run through its management training centres known as Hamburger University.
mcdonalds.hr.standardised-acquisition-an.use: Use for acquisition and development: show that crew training is specific rather than general, which shortens training time and protects consistency, then evaluate how well it builds skills for future roles.

mcdonalds.hr.maintenance-through-rosteri.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.maintenance-through-rosteri.label: Maintenance through rostering and grievance handling
mcdonalds.hr.maintenance-through-rosteri.fact: Rostering is the main maintenance tool in fast food. Crew commonly submit their availability each roster period so shifts can be built around school, study, sport and family commitments. Other maintenance measures typically include the rest and meal breaks set by the award, ongoing safety training, uniforms provided by the employer and an internal grievance procedure so problems reach a manager early. Because the franchisee is the legal employer, the detail varies between stores.
mcdonalds.hr.maintenance-through-rosteri.use: Use for the maintenance process and for social influences: argue flexible rostering is what keeps a student workforce, then link it to lower absenteeism and turnover when you judge effectiveness.

mcdonalds.hr.separation-in-a-young-casua.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.separation-in-a-young-casua.label: Separation in a young casual workforce
mcdonalds.hr.separation-in-a-young-casua.fact: Fast food work is known for high staff turnover because much of the crew is young, casual and studying, so most separations are voluntary resignations when a student finishes school, moves away or takes a job in their field. Involuntary separation is usually dismissal for breaching set procedures, such as food safety or attendance rules, and it must follow warnings and a fair process to avoid an unfair dismissal claim.
mcdonalds.hr.separation-in-a-young-casua.use: Use for the separation process: distinguish voluntary from involuntary separation in this workforce, then argue that high voluntary turnover is why induction and training are designed to be short and standardised.

mcdonalds.hr.leadership-style-on-a-shift.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.leadership-style-on-a-shift.label: Leadership style on a shift
mcdonalds.hr.leadership-style-on-a-shift.fact: Because procedures are set centrally and a shift is fast moving, day to day supervision is directive: the shift manager assigns stations and gives instructions that are followed straight away, which is close to an autocratic style. Alongside this, crew trainers coach new staff and crew are usually consulted about their availability and station preferences, so the style is not purely autocratic. Store level leadership sits with the franchisee and their managers rather than with head office.
mcdonalds.hr.leadership-style-on-a-shift.use: Use for leadership style: argue a directive style suits speed, safety and standardisation at peak trade, then balance it with the coaching and consultation that keep a young workforce motivated.

mcdonalds.hr.job-design-using-specific-t.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.job-design-using-specific-t.label: Job design using specific tasks
mcdonalds.hr.job-design-using-specific-t.fact: At McDonald's, work is divided into narrow, highly specified tasks at fixed stations, with a set procedure for every product and every step. This is specific job design, sometimes called job specialisation: a new employee becomes productive quickly and quality stays consistent, but repetition can cause boredom and low motivation, so crew are commonly rotated between stations to widen their skills.
mcdonalds.hr.job-design-using-specific-t.use: Use for job design, general or specific tasks: argue specific tasks support speed and cost control, then use the motivation drawback and the move towards general tasks through rotation to reach a balanced judgement. Use the syllabus words specific tasks and general tasks.

mcdonalds.hr.internal-recruitment-and-pr.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.internal-recruitment-and-pr.label: Internal recruitment and promotion pathway
mcdonalds.hr.internal-recruitment-and-pr.fact: McDonald's is well known for promoting from within. A typical path runs from crew member to crew trainer, then shift manager, assistant manager and restaurant manager, and the business publicly promotes the fact that many of its restaurant managers began as crew. Crew recruitment is external and looks for general skills, while management roles are usually filled internally, although exact titles vary between countries.
mcdonalds.hr.internal-recruitment-and-pr.use: Use for recruitment, internal or external and general or specific skills: connect the promotion pathway to motivation, lower recruitment costs and retention, and offer it as evidence of a strong corporate culture.

mcdonalds.hr.performance-management-agai.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.performance-management-agai.label: Performance management against set standards
mcdonalds.hr.performance-management-agai.fact: Because every task has a set procedure, crew performance can be measured directly against station standards, service times, food safety checks and customer feedback, and observation by crew trainers and managers during shifts is the usual method. Results are used developmentally to decide who is trained on further stations or promoted to crew trainer, and administratively when hours, pay level or continued employment are decided. The exact appraisal process is set by each franchisee.
mcdonalds.hr.performance-management-agai.use: Use for performance management, developmental or administrative: argue standardisation makes performance easy to measure objectively, then judge whether the developmental or the administrative purpose is doing more for motivation.

mcdonalds.hr.monetary-and-non-monetary-r.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.monetary-and-non-monetary-r.label: Monetary and non monetary rewards
mcdonalds.hr.monetary-and-non-monetary-r.fact: Crew receive an hourly rate set by the award, including penalty rates for late nights, weekends and public holidays, which is the monetary reward. Non monetary rewards carry real weight and commonly include flexible rostering, discounted or free meals on shift, crew recognition awards, nationally recognised training and a visible promotion path, although the exact package is set by each franchisee.
mcdonalds.hr.monetary-and-non-monetary-r.use: Use for rewards, monetary and non monetary: argue non monetary rewards do the heavy lifting because award wages limit pay differentiation, link the variation back to the franchise structure, then judge the effect on retention and satisfaction.

mcdonalds.hr.global-staffing-with-local-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.global-staffing-with-local-.label: Global staffing with local employees
mcdonalds.hr.global-staffing-with-local-.fact: McDonald's operates restaurants in many countries and staffs them almost entirely with local employees, recruited under each country's own employment law and wage rates, while a much smaller number of head office and training roles move between countries. The global strategy is therefore mostly local supply of labour combined with globally standardised training systems and operating procedures.
mcdonalds.hr.global-staffing-with-local-.use: Use for global, costs, skills and supply: argue labour is sourced locally so wage costs and employment law differ by country, then evaluate how standardised training keeps quality consistent across those different labour markets.

mcdonalds.hr.workplace-disputes-in-fast-.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.workplace-disputes-in-fast-.label: Workplace disputes in fast food
mcdonalds.hr.workplace-disputes-in-fast-.fact: Disputes in fast food typically concern rostering, unpaid overtime, breaks and penalty rates. They are normally raised first through the store's internal grievance procedure with the manager, then through the union covering the industry if the employee is a member, and only reach a tribunal if negotiation fails. Large scale industrial action is uncommon in this industry because the workforce is young, casual and spread across many small worksites.
mcdonalds.hr.workplace-disputes-in-fast-.use: Use for workplace disputes and resolution: name the grievance procedure and negotiation as the first steps, explain why they suit a dispute about rostering, then judge courts and tribunals as the slower last resort.

mcdonalds.hr.turnover-and-benchmarking-a.subject: business_studies
mcdonalds.hr.turnover-and-benchmarking-a.label: Turnover and benchmarking across stores
mcdonalds.hr.turnover-and-benchmarking-a.fact: Fast food work is characterised by high staff turnover and a young casual workforce, so human resource management is judged on staff turnover, absenteeism, accidents and worker satisfaction. Because every restaurant runs the same systems, service speed, order accuracy and safety incidents can be compared store to store, while crew turnover and absenteeism are held by each franchisee, so those variables are usually benchmarked within a franchisee's own stores or against the fast food industry.
mcdonalds.hr.turnover-and-benchmarking-a.use: Use for indicators and benchmarking key variables: name turnover and absenteeism, explain that standardised systems make operational comparison possible but that employment data sits with the franchisee, then evaluate overall effectiveness.

business.operations.role-of-operations-m.subject: business_studies
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.point: strategic role of operations management – cost leadership, good/service differentiation
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.what: Operations is the business function that transforms inputs into outputs. Its strategic role means operations decisions are made to deliver the whole business's competitive advantage, which is whatever makes customers choose this business over its rivals, not just to keep the factory or store running. Cost leadership means aiming to be the lowest cost producer in the industry so the business can compete on price and still make a profit, achieved through standardisation, high volume and stripping waste out of every process. Good/service differentiation is two separate tasks. Differentiating a good means changing its physical features, quality, reliability, design, materials or packaging so buyers see it as distinct. Differentiating a service means varying the level of staff expertise, convenience, speed of delivery, customisation or after sales support. Cost per unit is the average cost of producing one item, and it is the number a cost leader attacks.
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.why: Operations is where a strategy is either delivered or lost: a cost leader must remove cost from every process, while a differentiator must build extra features, quality or service into the process. The two pull against each other, because differentiation almost always raises the cost per unit, so operations must know which advantage the business is built to deliver before it chooses its processes, technology and performance objectives.
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.exam: Expect explain or assess: how operations strategies create cost leadership or good/service differentiation. Treat differentiation of a good and of a service separately, and finish on the trade off, that differentiation raises cost per unit while cost leadership limits how far the product can be differentiated. Pairs with performance objectives and with a case study business.
