business.operations.role-of-operations-m.subject: business_studies
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.point: goods and/or services in different industries
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.what: Goods are tangible items that can be touched, stored and transported. Services are intangible acts, produced and consumed at the same time, so they cannot be stored. Operations therefore looks different industry by industry. Manufacturing, such as car assembly or food processing, produces standardised tangible goods, meaning every unit is identical and mass produced, so it manages inventory, plant layout and quality control before the item ever reaches a customer. Retail sells goods but adds service, so it manages stock turnover, that is how quickly stock sells and is replaced, plus customer contact at the point of sale. Fast food and hospitality produce a good that is made and consumed almost immediately with high customer contact, so it cannot be stored and speed matters most. Professional services such as accounting, law or consulting produce an intangible output that is customised, made to the individual client's requirements, where staff skills and knowledge are the main input and there is almost no inventory. Most businesses sit somewhere between a pure good and a pure service rather than at either extreme.
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.why: The nature of the output decides how operations is run. A goods producer can build stock ahead of demand and inspect quality before the customer sees it. A service provider must get it right in front of the customer and match capacity to demand, because an unsold service hour is gone forever and cannot be stored. Marks come from naming the industry and saying what changes in its inputs, processes and outputs.
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.exam: Expect distinguish or outline: goods against services, or describe operations in a named industry. Name at least two contrasting industries, such as manufacturing and a professional service, and say what changes in inputs, processes and outputs, instead of defining goods and services in the abstract.

business.operations.role-of-operations-m.subject: business_studies
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.point: interdependence with other key business functions
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.what: Interdependence means the four key business functions, operations, marketing, finance and human resources, depend on each other and none of them can meet the business objectives, the goals the business sets itself, on its own. Marketing tells operations what customers want, forecasts how much will sell and promises delivery times and quality. Finance provides and controls the budget for equipment, materials and wages, and reports whether operations is hitting its cost targets. Human resources recruits, trains and rosters the staff who run the transformation process. Operations tells the other three what can actually be produced, by when and at what cost. Coordination is the deliberate planning that keeps these decisions consistent with each other.
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.why: A decision in one function creates consequences in the others: if marketing promotes a product operations cannot supply, sales are lost and the brand is damaged; if finance refuses capital, operations cannot buy the equipment the promotion assumed. Answers earn marks by naming the other function, saying what it supplies to operations and what operations supplies back, then giving one consequence when the link fails.
business.operations.role-of-operations-m.exam: Expect explain or describe interdependence, attached to another dot point such as new product or service design and development or a change in technology. Work through the functions one at a time rather than listing them, and end with what goes wrong when one is not ready.

business.operations.influences.globalisa.subject: business_studies
business.operations.influences.globalisa.point: globalisation, technology, quality expectations, cost-based competition, government policies, legal regulation, environmental sustainability
business.operations.influences.globalisa.what: Seven external influences shape operations. Globalisation is the world operating as one market, so a business can sell and buy inputs overseas but also meets overseas competitors at home, and must decide what to standardise and what to adapt. Technology, including computer aided design, computer aided manufacturing, automation and computerised stock control, raises speed, quality and flexibility and cuts labour cost per unit, but it needs capital investment and staff retraining. Quality expectations mean customers now expect fitness for purpose and reliability as a minimum, so businesses shift from inspecting faults out at the end towards quality assurance and continuous improvement. Cost-based competition is rivalry fought on price, which forces operations to standardise, cut waste and find cheaper inputs so it can survive at a lower price. Government policies are the direction and incentives government sets, including taxation, environmental policy, skills and training policy and industrial relations settings, which change what operations costs and how it may be run. Legal regulation is the binding rules operations must obey, such as work health and safety, fair trading, food safety and environmental protection law, where a breach brings penalties. The difference matters: policy sets direction and incentives, regulation sets rules that must be obeyed. Environmental sustainability is using resources so that future generations can still meet their needs, which pushes operations to cut waste, energy and packaging and to design products that can be reused or recycled.
business.operations.influences.globalisa.why: Influences are external, so operations cannot control them and can only respond. Each one changes the cost, the legality or the competitiveness of a process that already exists, and any of them can make a process illegal, obsolete or too expensive. The mark is earned by naming the influence and then the specific operational change it forces, such as new equipment, a new supplier, a new quality system or a redesigned product.
business.operations.influences.globalisa.exam: Expect analyse or discuss: how two or three influences affect operations. Choose influences you can carry into a strategy, for example cost-based competition into cost leadership and inventory management, or environmental sustainability into quality improvement and supply chain management. If both government policies and legal regulation appear, keep them apart.

business.operations.influences.corporate.subject: business_studies
business.operations.influences.corporate.what: Corporate social responsibility, or CSR, means the business takes responsibility for the effect of its operations on its stakeholders, that is any group affected by the business, on the community and on the environment, not only on profit. It has two levels. Legal compliance is the floor: obeying the laws that apply to operations, including work health and safety, environmental protection, consumer and fair trading law, food safety and employment law. Compliance is not optional and is not something to be praised for. Ethical responsibility sits above the floor: voluntary action that no law requires, such as cutting packaging further than the law demands, paying suppliers fairly and on time, or refusing an input that is legal but produced in poor conditions. The syllabus then splits the impact in two. Environmental sustainability is using resources so future generations can still meet their needs, for example cutting energy, water, waste and emissions. Social responsibility is fair treatment of workers, suppliers and the community, for example safe workplaces, honest labelling, local employment and community support.
business.operations.influences.corporate.why: CSR raises costs in the short term but protects what makes long term profit possible: reputation, customer loyalty, the ability to attract and keep staff, and freedom from fines, bans and damaging publicity. The distinction is also the trap in this dot point: calling something ethical when the law already requires it turns a strength into an error, so check whether an action is legally required before labelling it voluntary.
business.operations.influences.corporate.exam: Expect distinguish between legal compliance and ethical responsibility, or evaluate a business's CSR. Give one example that the law requires and one that is genuinely voluntary, then judge whether the voluntary action is worth its cost. Bring in both environmental sustainability and social responsibility, because the syllabus names both.

business.operations.operations-processes.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-processes.what: Inputs are the resources put into the transformation process. Transformed resources are the ones that are changed or converted by the process: materials, meaning raw materials and components; information, meaning the data used to run and decide, such as orders, forecasts and stock records; and customers, whose own state is changed by a service, for example a passenger who is moved or a client who is advised. Transforming resources are the ones that do the changing and are not used up in it: human resources, meaning staff and their skills, and facilities, meaning the plant, machinery, buildings and equipment.
business.operations.operations-processes.why: The quality, cost and availability of inputs set a ceiling on outputs, because poor materials or untrained staff produce defects and delays that no later stage can fix. Input costs also decide whether cost leadership is even possible, and the mix of inputs shows what kind of business it is, since a service business relies far more on human resources and information than on materials.
business.operations.operations-processes.exam: Expect identify or outline the inputs of a named business, then explain the difference between transformed and transforming resources. Name all three transformed resources, because customers are the one students leave out, and carry the answer forward into transformation processes.

business.operations.operations-processes.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-processes.what: Transformation processes convert inputs into outputs, and four factors shape them. Volume is how much is produced, and high volume allows standardisation and a lower cost per unit. Variety is how many different products are made, and high variety needs flexible equipment and multiskilled staff. Variation in demand is how far demand rises and falls across a day, week or season, which must be matched by rosters, capacity and stock. Visibility, or customer contact, is how much of the process the customer sees, and where it is high, waiting time, staff presentation and layout must be managed. Sequencing is the order in which tasks are done; scheduling is when each task starts and finishes and who does it. A Gantt chart is a bar chart with the tasks listed down the side and time across the top, where the length of each bar shows how long a task takes, so a manager can see start and finish dates, which tasks overlap and whether work is behind. Critical path analysis is a diagram of tasks drawn in the order they must be done, showing which tasks depend on others; the critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks and therefore the shortest possible time to finish the whole job, so a delay on the critical path delays the entire project while a delay off it may not. Task design sets what each worker does, process layout is the physical arrangement of equipment and workstations, and technology is the equipment and systems used. Monitoring is measuring what is actually happening against targets using key performance indicators, which are the specific measures chosen to judge performance, such as defect rates, lead times, waste levels and stock levels. Control is comparing actual results with planned results and taking corrective action wherever there is a variance. Improvement is changing the process itself so performance keeps rising, rather than only returning to the old standard.
business.operations.operations-processes.why: These choices set the cost, speed and quality of everything the business sells. Volume, variety, variation and visibility decide what kind of process is possible at all; sequencing and scheduling prevent bottlenecks and idle time so the same inputs produce more output; and monitoring, control and improvement are what stop performance drifting once the process is running, because measuring without correcting changes nothing and correcting without improving only restores the old standard.
business.operations.operations-processes.exam: Expect explain the influence of volume, variety, variation in demand and visibility on a named business, or describe how Gantt charts and critical path analysis are used in sequencing and scheduling. If monitoring, control and improvement are asked, give a separate example of each and name the key performance indicator being measured.

business.operations.operations-processes.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-processes.what: Outputs are the finished goods and services delivered to the customer, and the syllabus focuses on two ways operations manages them. Customer service is meeting customer expectations before, during and after the sale, through knowledgeable staff, accurate orders, easy returns, quick responses to complaints and after sales support. Warranties are a promise by the business to repair, replace or refund a product that proves faulty within a stated period. In Australia the consumer guarantees in the Australian Consumer Law, which are rights the law gives every buyer, apply on top of any warranty the business chooses to offer, so a business cannot use its own warranty to remove them. Warranty claims and complaints are also data, because they show where the fault is in the inputs or in the transformation process.
business.operations.operations-processes.why: Outputs are the only part of operations the customer actually judges, so service quality and reliability decide repeat business and word of mouth. Warranties also work backwards into the process: a rising claim rate warns that supplier quality or quality control has slipped, and each claim costs the business twice, once for the original input and again for the repair, replacement or refund.
business.operations.operations-processes.exam: Expect outline outputs, then explain how customer service and warranties support the quality and dependability performance objectives. Strong answers close the loop by feeding warranty and complaint data back into monitoring, control and improvement.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: performance objectives – quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, customisation, cost
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Performance objectives are the specific goals operations is judged against, and there are six. Quality is fitness for purpose and reliability, meaning the product does what it is meant to do and keeps doing it. Speed is how quickly the business responds to an order and delivers it, measured as lead time, the time from order to delivery. Dependability is consistency, delivering the same standard on time every time. Flexibility is how quickly operations can change what it makes, how much it makes or how it makes it. Customisation is tailoring the output to an individual customer's requirements. Cost is minimising the cost per unit so the business can price competitively and still earn a profit.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: Performance objectives turn a broad strategy into targets that can be measured, so the business can prove whether an operations strategy worked. They also trade off against each other: customisation and flexibility usually raise cost per unit, and pushing speed too hard can cost quality, so a cost leader leads on cost and dependability while a differentiator leads on quality and customisation.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect assess or explain how operations strategies help a business achieve its performance objectives. Pair each strategy with the objective it serves, for example quality management with quality, inventory management with cost, supply chain management with dependability, then judge the trade off between the objectives.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: new product or service design and development
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: New product or service design and development is the process of creating new outputs or improving existing ones, driven by market research, which is gathering information about customer needs, competitors and trends. Product design decides what the product does, what it is made of, how it looks and how it will be produced, so design also decides its cost, its quality and how easily it can be made. Product development turns the design into a working product through prototypes, which are trial versions built to be tested, then testing, a trial production run and finally full production. For a service, design covers the steps the customer goes through, the staff skills needed and the technology that supports them.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: Most of a product's cost is locked in at the design stage, because the design fixes the materials, the number of components and the processes required, so a good design lowers cost and builds quality in rather than inspecting it in later. New and improved products also keep the business competitive as customer tastes, technology and regulation change, and this dot point is where operations depends most heavily on marketing, finance and human resources.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect explain how new product or service design and development supports performance objectives, or discuss its interdependence with marketing and finance. Say what changes inside operations, such as new equipment, new suppliers, new procedures and retrained staff, not simply that the product is new.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: supply chain management – logistics, e-commerce, global sourcing
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Supply chain management is coordinating every business and activity from the supplier of raw materials through to the final customer, so that goods, money and information flow smoothly. Logistics is the physical movement and storage of goods, covering transport, warehousing and distribution to the customer. E-commerce is buying and selling online, which links a business directly to suppliers and customers, allows ordering at any hour and gives live information on stock and orders. Global sourcing is buying inputs from suppliers anywhere in the world, chosen for price, quality, capability or availability rather than for being nearby.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: A coordinated supply chain lowers input and transport costs, cuts the stock the business must hold and lifts dependability, meaning delivery on time and to the same standard, because inputs arrive when they are needed. The risk is exposure: a long or global chain can be broken by a supplier failure, a shipping delay, an exchange rate movement or a tariff, and the business still carries the blame with its own customers.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect explain or evaluate how supply chain management affects cost and dependability. Deal with logistics, e-commerce and global sourcing separately, then weigh the cost saving from global sourcing against the added risk of a longer chain. Links to globalisation as an influence and to inventory management.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: outsourcing – advantages and disadvantages
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Outsourcing means contracting an outside business to perform a function the business used to do itself, such as payroll, information technology, cleaning, maintenance, logistics, call centres or manufacturing. It can be domestic outsourcing, to a provider in the same country, or offshore outsourcing, to a provider in another country. Advantages are lower cost, because a specialist provider spreads its own costs across many clients, access to expertise and technology the business does not have, extra capacity at short notice, and freedom to concentrate on core activities, the things the business does that give it its competitive advantage. Disadvantages are loss of direct control over quality and timing, risk to confidential data and intellectual property, redundancies that damage the morale of remaining staff, the ongoing cost of writing and monitoring contracts, and dependence on a provider that could fail or raise its price.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: Outsourcing converts fixed costs, which are paid no matter how much is produced, such as wages and equipment, into variable costs paid only when the service is used, which improves flexibility and cash flow. The trade off is control: the business is still responsible to its own customers for quality and delivery even though somebody else does the work, so the contract, the agreed standards and the monitoring must do the job that direct supervision used to do.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect discuss, assess or evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of outsourcing, so argue both sides and reach a judgement. Name the function being outsourced, because the answer for payroll is not the answer for manufacturing. Links to cost leadership, technology and human resources.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: technology – leading edge, established
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Technology in operations is the equipment, systems and knowledge used to transform inputs into outputs. It includes computer aided design, designing a product on a computer so changes can be tested before anything is built; computer aided manufacturing, where machinery is controlled by computer; robotics; automation, machinery performing tasks with little human input; and computerised stock and ordering systems. Leading edge technology is the most advanced technology available, used by few or no competitors yet. Established technology has been in wide use for some time, is proven and reliable, and is cheaper to buy, maintain and staff because people already know how to run it.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: Leading edge technology can create an advantage rivals cannot match yet in speed, quality, flexibility or customisation, but it is expensive, unproven, needs retraining and can date quickly, so the business carries the cost and risk of being first. Established technology is low risk and cheap but delivers no advantage over competitors using the same tools. Most businesses run both, and today's leading edge becomes established once the industry adopts it.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect compare leading edge with established technology, or assess a technology investment. Judge it against cost, quality, speed and flexibility, and carry in the financial cost and retraining from overcoming resistance to change.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: inventory management – advantages and disadvantages of holding stock, LIFO (last-in-first-out), FIFO (first-in-first-out), JIT (just-in-time)
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Inventory is the stock a business holds: raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. Holding stock has advantages: orders can be filled at once so no sale is lost to a stockout, production continues when a supplier is late, unexpected demand can be met, and bulk buying usually earns a discount. It also has disadvantages: storage, handling and insurance cost money, cash is tied up in stock instead of being used elsewhere, and stock can spoil, be damaged, be stolen or suffer obsolescence, meaning it goes out of date and can no longer be sold at full price. LIFO, last in first out, and FIFO, first in first out, are assumptions about which stock cost is charged to the cost of goods sold, the cost of the stock actually sold in the period, and not necessarily how stock physically moves. When prices are rising, LIFO charges the newer higher cost, so cost of goods sold is higher and reported profit is lower, while FIFO charges the older lower cost, so cost of goods sold is lower and reported profit is higher. FIFO also matches the physical rotation businesses use for perishable or dated stock. JIT, just in time, means inputs arrive only as they are needed and the product is made only once it is ordered, so almost no stock is held.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: Inventory is one of the largest current assets a business holds, so the amount carried decides how much cash is locked up and how much cost is added. JIT cuts holding costs, storage space and waste and exposes process problems quickly, but it removes the buffer, so one late delivery or one disruption stops production and sales immediately, which is why JIT depends on reliable suppliers and a dependable supply chain.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect explain LIFO against FIFO, or discuss the advantages and disadvantages of holding stock and of just in time. For LIFO and FIFO, state the effect on cost of goods sold and on reported profit when prices are rising. Links to supply chain management and to the cost performance objective.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: quality management
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Quality management is everything a business does to make sure its output meets customer expectations. Quality control is inspecting and testing at set points during and after production to find defects, so faults are detected after they occur and the item is scrapped or reworked. Quality assurance is setting and following a system of standards and procedures, which are agreed specifications the process and product must meet, sometimes certified against an external standard, so faults are prevented rather than found and the business can prove the process was followed. Quality improvement is the ongoing search for a better process through continuous improvement, meaning many small changes made constantly by all employees rather than one large change made occasionally.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: A defect costs the business twice, once in the wasted input and again in the rework, refund or warranty claim, and a third time in reputation if the customer sees it. Preventing faults through assurance and improvement is cheaper than inspecting them out at the end, which is why the emphasis has moved from control towards assurance and improvement, and why quality management supports cost leadership through less waste and differentiation through reliability.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect distinguish between control, assurance and improvement, or evaluate quality management against the quality performance objective. Give one example of each, then judge which prevents the most defects and at what cost.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: overcoming resistance to change – financial costs, purchasing new equipment, redundancy payments, retraining, reorganising plant layout, inertia
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Two different things make operational change hard. The first is the financial cost of making the change: purchasing new equipment, redundancy payments to employees whose jobs are no longer needed, retraining staff on the new system, reorganising plant layout, which is the physical arrangement of equipment and workstations, and the production lost while the changeover happens. The second is inertia, the human resistance to change, where managers and employees keep doing things the familiar way because they fear losing status, skills, job security or control, or simply because the old way is comfortable. Overcoming resistance means attacking both. Consult and communicate with staff early so they understand why the change is needed and what it means for them. Involve them in planning it, because people support what they help build. Fund the change properly so it is not left half done. Retrain before the changeover rather than after it. Use a trial or a staged rollout, changing one site or one line first, so problems are found cheaply and staff can see the new way working.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: A change that is technically correct still fails if the business cannot afford it or if the people who must run it will not use it. Separating the two barriers is what the dot point rewards, because financial costs are the cost of changing while inertia is human resistance to changing, and each needs a different response, money and planning for one, communication and training for the other.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect explain the financial costs of change and inertia, or assess how a business overcame resistance to change. Keep the two barriers apart, then name a specific strategy against each, and remember that overcoming is the verb in the dot point, so most of the answer belongs there. Links to technology and to human resources.

business.operations.operations-strategie.subject: business_studies
business.operations.operations-strategie.point: global factors – global sourcing, economies of scale, scanning and learning, research and development
business.operations.operations-strategie.what: Global factors are the operational advantages a business gains by working on a world scale. Global sourcing is buying inputs from suppliers anywhere in the world, chosen for price, quality, capability or availability. Economies of scale are the fall in cost per unit as output rises, because fixed costs such as equipment, design and administration are spread across more units and large orders earn supplier discounts, so this is where buying power belongs. Scanning and learning means continually watching global markets, competitors and suppliers and adopting the best practice found, that is the methods that produce the best results anywhere in the industry. Research and development is planned spending on creating new products and better processes, which a global business can trial in one market before using everywhere.
business.operations.operations-strategie.why: Global scale lowers cost per unit and opens access to ideas, skills and technology that do not exist at home, so a global business can be both cheaper and better informed than a local rival. The risks are that a longer supply chain is more exposed to disruption, exchange rates and tariffs, and that a product or method accepted in one market may be rejected in another, which is why scanning and learning and research and development matter as much as scale.
business.operations.operations-strategie.exam: Expect analyse or evaluate how global factors improve operations. Cover all four, tie economies of scale to the cost objective and scanning and learning to quality or new products, and do not label bulk buying power as global sourcing. Links to globalisation as an influence and to cost leadership.

business.marketing.role-of-marketing.str.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.str.point: strategic role of marketing goods and services
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.str.what: Marketing is the process of identifying customer needs and satisfying them profitably. Goods are tangible items the customer can touch, services are intangible acts performed for the customer, and most businesses sell a mix of both. The strategic role of marketing is to build a competitive advantage, meaning a strength rivals cannot easily copy, by creating customer awareness, brand loyalty, meaning customers who keep choosing the same brand, and market share, meaning the business's percentage of total industry sales.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.str.why: Without marketing, even a good product fails because customers do not know it exists or why it beats rivals. Effective marketing lifts sales revenue, supports a higher price through brand loyalty, and drives the long term business objectives of profit, growth and market share, which is why it is called a strategic role rather than just selling.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.str.exam: Usually "outline" or "explain the strategic role of marketing", often linked to business objectives, market share or profit in short answer questions.

business.marketing.role-of-marketing.int.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.int.point: interdependence with other key business functions
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.int.what: The key business functions are operations, marketing, finance and human resources. Interdependence means each one relies on the others, so marketing cannot work alone: it depends on operations to produce and deliver what is promoted, on finance to fund advertising and to set prices that cover costs, and on human resources to recruit and train the staff who sell and serve. Information flows both ways, for example marketing passes sales forecasts to operations so the right volume is produced.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.int.why: If marketing promises delivery operations cannot meet, or promotes at a price finance cannot afford, customers are disappointed and profit falls. Coordinated functions mean campaigns are realistic, stock is available and staff can deliver the service that was promised.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.int.exam: Commonly "explain the interdependence of marketing with other key business functions", usually asking you to link marketing decisions to operations, finance and human resources.

business.marketing.role-of-marketing.pro.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.pro.what: The production approach focuses on making large volumes cheaply, assuming anything made will sell. The selling approach uses heavy advertising and personal selling to push products the business has already made. The marketing approach starts by researching customer needs, then designs the product to satisfy them. It is built on the marketing concept, the philosophy that every part of the business is directed at satisfying customer needs while still meeting business objectives such as profit. Although the three approaches developed in that order over time, businesses today still use all three: a commodity producer may still use a production approach.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.pro.why: A production or selling approach risks making goods nobody wants, wasting resources and leaving unsold inventory. A marketing approach, supported by relationship marketing, which is building long term ties with existing customers so they keep buying, produces repeat custom and loyalty because the product genuinely matches what the market asked for.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.pro.exam: Often "distinguish between" or "compare" the three approaches, or asked to identify which approach a stimulus business is using and evaluate it.

business.marketing.role-of-marketing.typ.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.typ.point: types of markets – resource, industrial, intermediate, consumer, mass, niche
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.typ.what: A market is all the buyers and sellers of a particular good or service, and the types are classified by who is buying and what they do with the purchase. Resource markets are the buyers and sellers of the inputs used in production: raw materials, primary products, labour and capital. Industrial markets are businesses that buy goods to use in producing other goods, such as a bakery buying ovens. Intermediate markets are wholesalers and retailers who buy finished goods in order to resell them at a profit. Consumer markets are individuals buying for their own personal use. Mass markets are where a business sells one product to as many buyers as possible; niche markets are one narrow, specialised segment.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.typ.why: The market type decides the whole marketing mix, because a niche market allows premium pricing and specialised promotion, while a mass market needs low unit cost, wide distribution and broad advertising to reach high volume. Classify a stimulus business by who its buyers are, not by what it sells.
business.marketing.role-of-marketing.typ.exam: Typically short answer "identify" or "outline types of markets", or multiple choice classifying a given business into a market type.

business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.point: factors influencing customer choice – psychological, sociocultural, economic, government
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.what: Consumer behaviour is how individuals decide what, when, where and why to buy, and four groups of factors shape that customer choice. Psychological factors are inside the buyer: perception, motives, attitudes, personality and learning. Sociocultural factors are outside social pressures: family, peers, social class and culture. Economic factors are the state of the economy, such as a boom lifting spending or a downturn tightening household budgets. Government factors are the laws, taxes and regulations that shape what can be sold, to whom, and how it may be advertised.
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.why: Understanding these factors lets a business target the right segment and time its campaigns, because during a downturn customers trade down to cheaper brands, so pricing and promotion must change or sales are lost. It also warns the business which changes it cannot control and must simply respond to.
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.exam: Very common as "explain how factors influence customer choice", or a stimulus asking you to analyse two factors affecting a named business's customers.

business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.what: Consumer laws protect buyers from unfair practice. Deceptive and misleading advertising is any claim or image likely to create a false impression, even if it is literally true. Price discrimination is charging different buyers different prices for the same good where this lessens competition. Implied conditions are unwritten guarantees that automatically apply to every sale by law: the good must be fit for its purpose, match its description and be of acceptable quality, and the seller cannot contract out of them. A warranty is an extra promise the seller or manufacturer voluntarily makes on top of those legal rights, usually for a stated time, to repair, replace or refund a faulty good.
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.why: Breaching consumer law brings penalties, legal costs and damaging publicity that destroys brand reputation, so compliance protects both customers and the business. Honouring implied conditions and warranties also builds the trust that produces repeat purchase.
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.exam: Frequently "outline" or "explain how consumer laws influence marketing", often paired with ethical marketing in an extended response on influences.

business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.point: ethical – truth, accuracy and good taste in advertising, products that may damage health, engaging in fair competition, sugging
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.what: Ethical marketing goes beyond legal compliance to what is fair and socially responsible. Truth, accuracy and good taste means advertising must not exaggerate, offend or exploit fear. Products that may damage health, such as tobacco, alcohol, gambling and high kilojoule food, raise the question of whether a business should promote them at all, and to whom. Engaging in fair competition means winning on merit rather than through misleading conduct or predatory tactics. Sugging is selling under the guise of research, that is, pretending to run a survey in order to make a sale.
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.why: Unethical marketing may lift short term sales but risks consumer backlash, boycotts and tighter regulation, which cost far more than the extra revenue. Ethical conduct protects reputation and supports long term customer loyalty and market share, although it can raise costs and rule out profitable segments, which is the tension you weigh in an evaluate question.
business.marketing.influences-on-marketi.exam: Often "assess the ethical influences on marketing" or "discuss", requiring you to weigh profit against social responsibility, usually alongside consumer laws.

business.marketing.marketing-process.sit.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-process.sit.point: situational analysis – SWOT, product life cycle
business.marketing.marketing-process.sit.what: Situational analysis is the first step of the marketing plan: examining where the business stands now. SWOT audits internal strengths and weaknesses, which the business controls, and external opportunities and threats, which it does not. The product life cycle tracks a product through introduction, growth, maturity and decline, and each stage needs different product, price and promotion decisions. Extension strategies are actions taken in the maturity stage to lift sales before decline sets in, such as restyling or repackaging the product, adding new features or flavours, finding new market segments, running limited time offers, or cutting the price.
business.marketing.marketing-process.sit.why: Knowing the current position stops the business setting unrealistic objectives. Spotting a product entering decline lets managers apply an extension strategy or launch a replacement before revenue collapses, which protects market share and profit.
business.marketing.marketing-process.sit.exam: Commonly "explain the role of situational analysis" or a stimulus SWOT table you must interpret, plus identifying a product's life cycle stage.

business.marketing.marketing-process.mar.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-process.mar.what: Market research is the systematic collecting, recording and analysing of data about customers, competitors and the market, and it runs in three steps. First, determining information needs, meaning deciding exactly what the business must find out and why. Second, collecting data: primary data is gathered first hand for this problem through surveys, observation and experiments, while secondary data already exists, such as internal sales records, government statistics and published industry reports. Third, data analysis and interpretation, turning raw findings into conclusions that become market objectives and strategies.
business.marketing.marketing-process.mar.why: Research replaces guessing with evidence, so the business develops products customers actually want and cuts the risk of an expensive failed launch. It also uncovers unmet needs that become new market opportunities, and gives the benchmark data used later to compare actual with planned results.
business.marketing.marketing-process.mar.exam: Usually "outline the steps in market research" or "explain how market research informs marketing strategies", sometimes with survey data as stimulus.

business.marketing.marketing-process.est.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-process.est.what: Market objectives are the specific, measurable goals the marketing plan must achieve, such as increasing market share, which is the business's percentage of total industry sales, growing sales revenue, which is price multiplied by quantity sold, expanding the product range, maximising customer service, or entering a new market. They should be realistic and time bound, for example lifting market share by a set amount within twelve months, and they must support the overall business objectives of profit, growth, market share and social responsibility.
business.marketing.marketing-process.est.why: Objectives give direction and a benchmark, because without a measurable target the business cannot judge whether a campaign worked. They also guide how the marketing budget is divided and let managers compare actual results against planned results.
business.marketing.marketing-process.est.exam: Short answer "identify market objectives" or an extended response where you must state an objective before recommending strategies to achieve it.

business.marketing.marketing-process.ide.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-process.ide.what: A target market is the group of customers a business aims its marketing mix at, that is, its product, price, promotion and place decisions. It is found by market segmentation, dividing the total market into groups with similar characteristics, then choosing an approach: mass marketing, one mix aimed at the whole market; a market segmentation approach, targeting several segments with a different mix for each; or a niche approach, concentrating on one small, specialised segment, known as a niche market.
business.marketing.marketing-process.ide.why: Targeting concentrates a limited marketing budget on the customers most likely to buy, which raises the return on promotional spending and lets product, price and place be tailored precisely to that group. Choosing a niche also reduces direct competition, although it limits total volume.
business.marketing.marketing-process.ide.exam: Often "explain how a business identifies its target market", or stimulus asking you to recommend a target market and justify the choice.

business.marketing.marketing-process.dev.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-process.dev.what: Marketing strategies are the actions taken to achieve the market objectives, and this step turns those objectives into the marketing mix: product, the total offering including quality, features and branding; price, what is charged and by which method; promotion, how the offering is communicated to the target market; and place, how the product reaches the customer. Service businesses add people, processes and physical evidence. Strategies must suit the target market, the product life cycle stage and the budget, and every element must be consistent with the others.
business.marketing.marketing-process.dev.why: A mismatched mix confuses customers, for example a premium price with cheap packaging sold through discount outlets, which weakens positioning. A consistent mix reinforces the brand image and converts research and objectives into actual sales.
business.marketing.marketing-process.dev.exam: Very common in extended response: "recommend marketing strategies a business could use", requiring you to justify each element of the mix.

business.marketing.marketing-process.imp.subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-process.imp.point: implementation, monitoring and controlling – developing a financial forecast; comparing actual and planned results, revising the marketing strategy
business.marketing.marketing-process.imp.what: Implementation puts the strategies into practice, assigning who does what, by when and with what budget. A financial forecast predicts sales revenue and marketing costs so a budget can be set. Monitoring is checking progress against that plan as it happens, using sales figures, market share data and customer feedback. Controlling compares actual results with planned results, and where there is a variance the cause is found and the marketing strategy is revised, for example by changing the promotion, the price or the target market.
business.marketing.marketing-process.imp.why: Markets change quickly, so a plan left unchecked wastes money on strategies that no longer work. Comparing actual with planned results catches underperformance early, letting the business revise the mix while there is still time to meet the objective.
business.marketing.marketing-process.imp.exam: Usually "explain the process of monitoring and controlling" or stimulus with forecast versus actual sales, asking you to recommend revisions.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..point: market segmentation, product/service differentiation and positioning
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: Market segmentation divides the total market into groups with similar characteristics, using demographic variables such as age, gender, income and family size, geographic variables such as where customers live, psychographic variables such as lifestyle, values and personality, and behavioural variables such as how often and why they buy. Product/service differentiation makes the offering distinct from rivals through quality, features, packaging or service. Positioning is the image the product holds in the customer's mind relative to competitors, for example the cheapest, the fastest or the most premium. The segment or segments the business decides to aim its mix at become its target market.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: Segmentation lets the mix be tailored so promotion reaches the right people, while differentiation and positioning justify a higher price and build loyalty, because customers see no close substitute and become less sensitive to price.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Frequently "explain how segmentation, differentiation and positioning work together", or "analyse" their effect on a business's competitiveness.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: The product is the total offering: the good or service itself plus quality, features, brand and after sales support. Branding is the name, term, symbol or design that identifies a product and separates it from rivals, building brand recognition and brand loyalty, meaning customers who keep choosing the same brand instead of switching. Packaging is the container and wrapper, which protects the product, promotes it through colour, shape and design, and identifies it on a crowded shelf. Both are tools of product differentiation, making the offering stand out from close substitutes.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: A strong brand lets the business charge a premium price and launch new products more easily because customers already trust the name. Packaging attracts attention at the point of sale and can differentiate an otherwise almost identical product.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Often "explain the role of branding and packaging as marketing strategies", or asked to recommend product strategies within a full marketing mix answer.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..point: price including pricing methods – cost, market, competition-based
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: Cost based pricing adds a mark up to the cost of production. Market based pricing sets the price according to supply and demand. Competition based pricing sets the price at, above or below what rivals charge. The strategies are: skimming, a high launch price while the product is new and has few rivals; penetration, a low launch price to win market share quickly; loss leaders, items sold at or below cost to draw customers in, expecting them to buy other items too; and price points, offering products at a small number of set price levels, for example a value range, a standard range and a premium range, so customers can quickly compare tiers and trade up. Price and quality interaction means customers use price as a signal of quality, so the price must be high enough to look credible for the quality claimed.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: Price directly sets sales revenue and must cover costs, but it also positions the product, because a price that is too low can signal poor quality and undermine a premium image, while a price above what the target market will pay loses volume to rivals.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Commonly "explain" or "compare pricing methods and strategies", or stimulus asking you to recommend a pricing strategy for a new product and justify it.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: Promotion communicates with the target market through four elements of the promotion mix. Advertising is paid, non personal messaging through mass media. Personal selling is staff dealing directly with a buyer, and relationship marketing builds long term ties so that customer keeps returning. Sales promotions are short term incentives such as coupons, competitions, samples and limited time offers. Publicity is free media coverage of the business, while public relations are the activities the business runs, such as sponsorship and community events, to earn that coverage and protect its image. The communication process is how the message travels: the business is the sender, it encodes a message, sends it through a medium such as television, social media or a billboard, and the target market receives and decodes it, then gives feedback through sales or comments. Noise, meaning competing messages, can block it. An opinion leader is a person whose views others respect and copy, such as an athlete, a chef or a social media influencer, so their endorsement carries more weight than an advertisement, and word of mouth is customers telling other people about their own experience.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: Promotion creates awareness and interest and moves customers towards purchase, which lifts sales. Opinion leaders and positive word of mouth are especially powerful because customers trust independent people far more than paid advertising, but the business cannot control the message once it is passed on, and negative word of mouth spreads just as fast.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Very common: "explain the elements of the promotion mix" or "recommend promotional strategies", often needing the communication process and word of mouth.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: Place is getting the product to the customer at the right time and location. Distribution channels are the routes used, such as producer direct to consumer, or producer to retailer to consumer, or producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. Channel choice can be intensive, using as many outlets as possible, selective, using a limited number of chosen outlets, or exclusive, using one outlet in each area. Physical distribution covers transport, moving the goods, warehousing, storing them close to demand, and inventory, deciding how much stock to hold.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: The channel affects availability, cost and image, because exclusive distribution supports a luxury position while intensive distribution maximises convenience and volume. Poor transport, warehousing or inventory decisions cause stockouts that lose sales, or high holding costs that erode profit.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Often "explain channel choice" or asked in a mix recommendation to justify intensive, selective or exclusive distribution for a given product.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: These are the extra elements of the services marketing mix. People are the staff the customer deals with directly, so their skills, knowledge, appearance and attitude are part of the product. Processes are the systems and flow that deliver the service, such as booking, ordering, queuing and payment. Physical evidence is the tangible surroundings the customer can actually see and judge: the premises, layout, uniforms, signage, packaging and equipment.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: Services are intangible, meaning the customer cannot see, touch or test them before buying, so they judge quality by the staff, the smoothness of the process and the physical surroundings. Getting these right differentiates the service and builds repeat business, while rude staff or slow processes lose customers immediately.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Usually appears in service business stimulus: "explain how people, processes and physical evidence can be used as marketing strategies".

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: E-marketing is using the internet and digital technology to market goods and services. It includes a business website and online store where customers browse, order and pay, email campaigns, social media pages that carry content and let customers reply publicly, search and display advertising, and mobile apps. It allows two way communication, personalised offers based on the customer's own browsing and purchase data, and selling twenty four hours a day to a global audience.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: E-marketing cuts distribution and promotion costs, reaches customers far beyond the local area and gives fast feedback through data on clicks, sales and comments, which makes monitoring and controlling easier. However it raises privacy, data security and trust issues, and a public complaint can spread quickly, so it must be managed.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Typically "evaluate the effectiveness of e-marketing" or "explain how e-marketing can help achieve marketing objectives", weighing benefits against privacy concerns.

business.marketing.marketing-strategies..subject: business_studies
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..what: Global marketing is marketing goods and services in overseas markets. Global branding uses one name, logo and image worldwide. Standardisation keeps the same product and promotion in every market to cut costs and gain economies of scale. Customisation adapts the product or promotion to local tastes, culture and laws. Global pricing has three approaches: customised pricing sets a different price in each market based on that market's own costs of production and distribution; market customised pricing sets the price according to what each local market will bear, based on local demand, incomes and competition; and transfer pricing is the price charged when goods move between the business's own divisions in different countries, which can be set to shift profit towards lower tax countries. Competitive positioning is deciding how the brand should be seen against global rivals, for example as the cheapest, the fastest or the most premium, then making the mix in every market support that image.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..why: Going global grows sales and spreads risk across several markets. Standardisation gains economies of scale and one consistent image, although customisation may be needed because cultural, legal and language differences mean an unchanged product can fail or offend in a new market, so most global businesses blend the two.
business.marketing.marketing-strategies..exam: Common in extended response: "discuss" or "evaluate global marketing strategies", especially weighing standardisation against customisation for a named business.

business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.subject: business_studies
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.what: Financial management is planning, monitoring and controlling a business's financial resources, the funds and assets it has to work with, so the business meets its objectives, the goals it sets itself such as profit, growth, market share and meeting shareholder expectations. Its strategic role is long-term: deciding how much finance is needed, where it comes from and what it is spent on, so the business stays profitable and stays solvent, meaning able to meet its long-term commitments.
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.why: Without financial management a business can be profitable on paper yet still collapse because it cannot pay wages or suppliers. Sound financial decisions fund growth, control costs and keep the business solvent, so finance shapes what every other part of the business is able to do.
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.exam: Usually "explain" or "discuss" the strategic role, most often paired with objectives of financial management or with interdependence between finance and other functions.

business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.subject: business_studies
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.what: Profitability is earning a return above costs. Growth is increasing the size and value of the business. Efficiency is using assets and controlling expenses well. Liquidity is meeting short-term debts as they fall due. Solvency is meeting long-term commitments. Short-term objectives are tactical and operational, usually set for a year or less; long-term objectives are strategic and set for two years or more.
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.why: Objectives give measurable targets that financial ratios can test, and they conflict, so managers must trade them off. Chasing rapid growth can drain liquidity, so a business balances short-term survival against long-term return.
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.exam: "Explain" or "assess" how a business achieves its objectives, almost always requiring financial ratios as evidence, or a stated conflict between liquidity and profitability.

business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.subject: business_studies
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.point: interdependence with other key business functions
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.what: Finance both depends on and supports operations, marketing and human resources. Finance sets and approves the budgets, the planned allocations of funds, that those functions spend, and their activity creates the revenue, the income earned from sales, and the expenses, the costs of operating, that finance reports on. Operations needs funds for equipment and inputs, marketing for promotion and market research, human resources for wages and training.
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.why: A decision in one function immediately changes the finances of the others, so poor coordination causes budget blowouts, cash shortages or lost sales, while good coordination directs scarce funds where the return is highest.
business.finance.role-of-financial-manag.exam: "Explain the interdependence between finance and one other function." Markers want influence in both directions, not just finance handing out money.

business.finance.influences-on-financial.subject: business_studies
business.finance.influences-on-financial.point: internal sources of finance – retained profits
business.finance.influences-on-financial.what: Internal finance comes from inside the business rather than from outside lenders or investors. The main internal source is retained profits: net profit, which is revenue less all expenses, that is kept in the business instead of being paid out to owners or shareholders as dividends, the share of profit distributed to them. Retained profits are cheap and flexible, need no lender's approval, and carry no interest or repayment obligation.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.why: Retained profits cost no interest and dilute no ownership, so they lower gearing, the proportion of debt to equity in the business, and reduce financial risk. However, relying on them limits how fast a business can grow and can frustrate shareholders who want higher dividends now.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.exam: Usually set against external sources in "compare" or "evaluate" questions about choosing the best source of finance for a stated purpose.

business.finance.influences-on-financial.subject: business_studies
business.finance.influences-on-financial.what: External finance comes from outside the business. Debt is borrowed and repaid with interest. Short-term borrowing includes an overdraft, which lets a business overdraw its account to an agreed limit; commercial bills, larger short-term loans repaid on a set date; and factoring, selling accounts receivable to a finance company for immediate cash. Long-term borrowing includes a mortgage, a loan secured against property; debentures, secured loans to a company at a fixed rate and term; unsecured notes, the same without security; and leasing, paying to use an asset owned by someone else. Equity is funds from owners: ordinary shares raised through new issues, rights issues offered to existing shareholders, placements to selected investors and share purchase plans, plus private equity, funds from private investors rather than a public market.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.why: External finance lets a business buy assets and expand beyond what its own profits allow. Debt raises gearing and interest costs but keeps control with existing owners, while equity carries no repayment obligation but dilutes ownership and shares future profits.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.exam: "Outline" or "compare" named sources, or a case study choosing finance for a purchase. Use the exact source names and match the term of the finance to the purpose.

business.finance.influences-on-financial.subject: business_studies
business.finance.influences-on-financial.point: financial institutions – banks, investment banks, finance companies, superannuation funds, life insurance companies, unit trusts and the Australian Securities Exchange
business.finance.influences-on-financial.what: Banks accept deposits and are the main lender to business, providing overdrafts, loans and mortgages. Investment banks advise on and arrange large raisings, share issues and takeovers for companies rather than taking retail deposits. Finance companies provide leasing, hire purchase and personal or small business loans, and raise their own funds by issuing debentures. Superannuation funds invest compulsory employee contributions in shares, property and loans, which makes them a major supplier of funds to business. Life insurance companies invest the premium income they collect and lend to business. Unit trusts pool small investors' funds into one specified investment type such as property, shares or mortgages. The Australian Securities Exchange is the market where shares are issued and traded, giving companies access to equity and investors a way to sell.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.why: These institutions decide who receives funds, how much those funds cost and on what conditions, so their lending criteria and interest rates directly shape which projects a business can afford to finance.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.exam: "Outline the role of" a named institution, or "explain how financial institutions influence financial management." Learn one precise role for each, especially the Australian Securities Exchange.

business.finance.influences-on-financial.subject: business_studies
business.finance.influences-on-financial.point: influence of government – Australian Securities and Investments Commission, company taxation
business.finance.influences-on-financial.what: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission is the corporate regulator: it enforces the Corporations Act, oversees company registration, financial reporting and disclosure, which is the requirement to make accurate financial information available to shareholders and the market, and it investigates and acts against misleading or fraudulent conduct. Company taxation requires companies to pay tax on their profits, a cash outflow that reduces the funds left for retained profits and dividends.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.why: Regulation forces accurate reporting, which protects investors and lenders but adds compliance costs, the cost of meeting legal requirements such as audits, records and reports. Tax must be budgeted for, so tax rates and payment timing affect cash flow and after tax returns.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.exam: "Explain how government influences financial management." Answers normally need one paragraph on the Australian Securities and Investments Commission regulating reporting and disclosure, and one on company tax reducing available funds.

business.finance.influences-on-financial.point: global market influences – economic outlook, availability of funds, interest rates
business.finance.influences-on-financial.what: The economic outlook is the expected state of the world economy, which affects demand, business confidence and investment. Availability of funds is how easily, and on what conditions, a business can access finance in overseas capital markets; it tightens when lenders judge risk to be higher. Interest rates differ between countries, so borrowing overseas may be cheaper, but repayments are in a foreign currency, creating exchange rate risk, the risk that a currency movement raises the cost of those repayments.
business.finance.influences-on-financial.why: Global conditions set the price and supply of finance. Cheaper foreign funds cut costs, but a falling Australian dollar raises the cost of repaying foreign debt, and tight global credit can stall planned expansion.

business.finance.processes-of-financial-.subject: business_studies
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.point: planning and implementing – financial needs, budgets, record systems, financial risks, financial controls
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.what: Financial needs are worked out from the business's goals, its current financial position and any planned expansion. Budgets are planned allocations of funds: operating budgets for expected revenue and expenses, project budgets for one-off items such as a fit-out, and financial budgets for cash, capital expenditure and the projected balance sheet. Record systems are the procedures for recording and storing accurate financial data, such as sales, receipts, payments, invoices and payroll. Financial risk is the risk of not being able to cover debts as they fall due. Financial controls are policies and procedures, such as authorisation levels for spending, separation of duties, bank reconciliations and regular stocktakes, that protect assets from fraud, theft and waste. On debt: it can be arranged quickly and the interest paid on it is a tax deductible expense, which lowers its effective cost, but the principal must be repaid with interest whether or not the business is profitable, and it raises gearing and financial risk. On equity: it carries no repayment obligation and no interest, and it lowers gearing, but it dilutes ownership and control and shares future profits, and it is slower and more costly to raise. Matching the terms and source of finance to business purpose means using short-term finance for current assets and long-term finance for non-current assets.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.why: Without planning a business borrows the wrong money for the wrong period, paying long-term interest on a short-term need or facing repayment before the asset earns income. Controls also prevent fraud, theft and waste, and the debt or equity choice fixes how much repayment risk the business must carry in a downturn.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.exam: "Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of debt and equity financing" is a standard extended response. Give at least two advantages and two disadvantages of each, then use matching finance to purpose as the judgement.

business.finance.processes-of-financial-.point: monitoring and controlling – cash flow statement, income statement, balance sheet
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.what: The cash flow statement shows cash received and paid under operating, investing and financing activities over a period of time, usually a financial year, so it reveals liquidity. The income statement also covers a period of time, showing revenue less cost of goods sold to give gross profit, then less expenses to give net profit. The balance sheet is different: it is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a single point in time, usually the last day of that period. That is why the three are read together, because a snapshot cannot show performance across a year and a period report cannot show what the business owns and owes on a given day.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.why: These reports turn business activity into evidence. Monitoring compares actual results against budgets so managers act early, fixing a cash shortfall or rising expenses before the business becomes illiquid or unprofitable.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.exam: Expect to construct or read a statement and then interpret it, or "explain how monitoring and controlling improves financial performance." Always say which reports cover a period and which is a point in time.

business.finance.processes-of-financial-.subject: business_studies
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.what: Liquidity: current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Gearing: debt to equity ratio is total liabilities divided by total equity. Profitability: gross profit ratio is gross profit divided by sales; net profit ratio is net profit divided by sales; return on equity ratio is net profit divided by total equity. Efficiency: expense ratio is total expenses divided by sales; accounts receivable turnover ratio is sales divided by accounts receivable. Comparative ratio analysis then compares each result over different time periods, against standards such as an industry average, and with similar businesses.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.why: A single dollar figure means little on its own. Ratios convert the statements into comparable measures of liquidity, gearing, profitability and efficiency, and only a comparison shows whether performance is improving and exactly where a manager should intervene.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.exam: Ratio calculation followed by interpretation appears regularly in the short answer and stimulus based sections. State the formula, calculate, then interpret the result against a comparison over time, against a standard or with a similar business.

business.finance.processes-of-financial-.subject: business_studies
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.point: limitations of financial reports – normalised earnings, capitalising expenses, valuing assets, timing issues, debt repayments, notes to the financial statements
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.what: Normalised earnings remove one-off items to show underlying performance, but deciding which items are one-off is a judgement that can be used to flatter results. Capitalising expenses records a cost as an asset instead of an expense, which lifts reported profit now and pushes the cost into later years. Valuing assets relies on estimates, especially intangibles such as goodwill and brand names. Timing issues shift revenue or expenses between periods so one year looks stronger. Debt repayments are a limitation because the balance sheet shows the size of a liability but not the repayment schedule, so a business can appear solvent while a large repayment falls due within months, and a loan classified as non-current can still require significant repayments in the coming year. Notes to the financial statements disclose the accounting methods used, valuation and depreciation methods and contingent liabilities, so two businesses showing near identical statements can rest on very different assumptions, and ratios calculated without reading the notes can mislead.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.why: Reports look objective but rest on judgements, so ratios built from them can mislead investors and lenders. A user who ignores the notes or the timing of debt repayments can badly misjudge both liquidity and profitability.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.exam: "Explain the limitations of financial reports" or "assess their usefulness." Name at least three limitations and show how each distorts a specific decision by a lender, investor or manager.
