business.finance.processes-of-financial-.point: ethical issues related to financial reports
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.what: Ethical reporting means financial statements are honest, accurate and complete rather than technically legal but misleading. Unethical practices include window dressing, arranging transactions or presentation so the short-term position looks stronger than it is, understating expenses, hiding debt, misusing company funds and trading on inside information. Audited accounts are statements independently examined by an auditor, internal or external, who reports whether they give a true and fair view, meaning free of material misstatement and not misleading.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.why: Investors, lenders and employees rely on these reports to make decisions, so misleading figures destroy trust, can breach the Corporations Act, and lead to penalties, reputational damage and even business collapse.
business.finance.processes-of-financial-.exam: Usually "discuss ethical issues in financial reporting." Strong answers separate legal compliance from ethical responsibility and name auditing and disclosure as the safeguards.

business.finance.financial-management-st.subject: business_studies
business.finance.financial-management-st.what: Cash flow management ensures cash inflows cover outflows when they fall due. A cash flow statement records operating, investing and financing cash over a period. Strategies include distribution of payments, spreading large outflows such as insurance, rent and tax evenly through the year instead of letting them fall together; discounts for early payment, offering debtors a small price reduction to pay sooner; and factoring, selling accounts receivable to a finance company for immediate cash at a discount.
business.finance.financial-management-st.why: A profitable business still fails if it cannot pay wages, suppliers or loan instalments on time. Managing the timing of cash keeps the business liquid, avoids costly emergency overdrafts and protects its credit reputation.
business.finance.financial-management-st.exam: A very common "explain" or "recommend a strategy" question in case studies showing a cash shortage. Name the strategy and state its effect on the timing of cash.

business.finance.financial-management-st.subject: business_studies
business.finance.financial-management-st.what: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, the funds available for day to day operations. Control of current assets manages cash, receivables and inventories so none is excessive or short. Control of current liabilities manages payables, loans and overdrafts, for example by using supplier credit terms fully. Strategies include leasing, paying to use an asset instead of buying it, which avoids a large upfront outlay; and sale and lease back, selling an owned asset and then leasing it back from the buyer, which releases cash tied up in the asset while the business keeps using it.
business.finance.financial-management-st.why: Too little working capital means the business cannot pay its debts as they fall due; too much means idle cash and stock earning no return. Managing it balances liquidity against profitability.
business.finance.financial-management-st.exam: "Explain how working capital management improves liquidity", usually tied to the current ratio, or evaluate leasing against outright purchase.

business.finance.financial-management-st.subject: business_studies
business.finance.financial-management-st.what: Profitability management widens the gap between revenue and costs. Cost controls separate fixed costs, which do not change with the level of output, from variable costs, which do; use cost centres, areas of the business to which costs can be directly attributed and made accountable; and apply expense minimisation, cutting expenses without damaging quality. Revenue controls set marketing objectives such as sales targets, pricing decisions, market share and a sales mix.
business.finance.financial-management-st.why: Profit can be lifted from either side, so managers cut waste without damaging quality while raising sales volume or price. Cost centres also reveal exactly which part of the business is losing money.
business.finance.financial-management-st.exam: "Explain strategies to improve profitability", normally requiring both a cost strategy and a revenue strategy, and often linked to the gross profit and net profit ratios.

business.finance.financial-management-st.subject: business_studies
business.finance.financial-management-st.what: Exchange rates change the value of overseas receipts and payments, so a profit can be won or lost between the sale and the payment. Interest rates differ between countries, so borrowing offshore may be cheaper but adds currency risk. Methods of international payment run from payment in advance, safest for the exporter because the goods are not sent until paid, to letter of credit, a bank guarantee of payment, then bill of exchange, an order to pay on a set date, then clean payment, where goods are sent before payment and the exporter carries the most risk. Hedging reduces exchange rate risk, using derivatives, financial instruments whose value comes from an underlying asset or rate, such as futures, options and swaps, and natural methods such as invoicing in the home currency.
business.finance.financial-management-st.why: A currency movement can wipe out an export profit between the sale and the payment, so hedging and the choice of payment method decide how much risk a business carries when trading or borrowing overseas.
business.finance.financial-management-st.exam: A reliable extended response: "explain how a business manages global financial risk." Rank the payment methods by risk and name specific derivatives.

business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.subject: business_studies
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.what: Human resource management is the management of the total relationship between employer and employee, from hiring through to separation. Its strategic role is to align the workforce with the long term business plan through effective acquisition, development, maintenance and separation of staff, so that employees become a source of competitive advantage, meaning something the business does better than its rivals that customers are willing to pay for.
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.why: Employees deliver the quality, service and innovation customers pay for, so a skilled and committed workforce lifts productivity, which is output produced per worker per hour, and cuts the cost of turnover, while weak human resource management causes disputes, absenteeism and loss of corporate knowledge.
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.exam: Asked as explain or discuss the strategic role of human resources, usually paired with business performance or with the other key business functions.

business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.subject: business_studies
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.point: interdependence with other key business functions
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.what: Human resource management cannot work alone because it depends on and shapes the other key business functions, which are operations, marketing and finance. Operations needs skilled staff to run transformation processes, marketing needs trained staff to deliver customer service, and finance sets the budget available for wages, training and rewards. A change in one function changes staffing needs in all of them, which is what interdependence means.
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.why: Ignoring interdependence makes plans fail, because a marketing campaign that lifts demand without extra trained staff damages service quality, and a finance decision to cut training reduces operational quality and safety.
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.exam: Asked as explain or analyse the interdependence between human resources and one other function, in short answer and inside extended responses.

business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.subject: business_studies
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.what: Outsourcing means paying an outside provider to do work once done inside the business. Human resource functions such as recruitment, payroll, training and workplace relations advice can be outsourced to specialists. Contractors are engaged under a contract for a task or a result rather than employed, and may be domestic, meaning based in Australia, or global, meaning based overseas where labour is cheaper.
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.why: Outsourcing converts fixed labour costs into variable costs and buys specialist expertise and flexibility, although it reduces direct control over quality, can weaken corporate culture and creates ethical and legal risk when global contractors use unsafe or exploitative conditions.
business.hr.role-of-human-resource-manag.exam: Asked as assess or evaluate the use of outsourcing, paired with cost, flexibility, control and with ethics and corporate social responsibility.

business.hr.key-influences.stakeholders.subject: business_studies
business.hr.key-influences.stakeholders.point: stakeholders – employers, employees, employer associations, unions, government organisations, society
business.hr.key-influences.stakeholders.what: Stakeholders are groups with an interest in human resource decisions. Employers direct work and pay wages. Employees supply labour and seek fair pay, security and safety. Employer associations are organisations that advise and represent employers in workplace relations. Unions are organisations that represent employees collectively and bargain on their behalf. Government organisations make and enforce workplace law and hear disputes. Society expects safe, fair and non discriminatory employment.
business.hr.key-influences.stakeholders.why: Stakeholder interests conflict, because employees want higher wages and employers want lower costs, so managers must balance them to avoid industrial disputes, legal action and damage to the business reputation.
business.hr.key-influences.stakeholders.exam: Asked as outline, describe or examine the role and conflicting interests of stakeholders, often with stimulus material showing a workplace dispute.

business.hr.key-influences.legal.subject: business_studies
business.hr.key-influences.legal.what: The employment contract is a common law agreement, meaning it is built on judge made law: the employer must pay the agreed wage, provide a safe workplace and reimburse work expenses, while the employee must obey lawful and reasonable instructions, work with care and skill and act in good faith. Minimum employment standards, such as maximum weekly hours, leave and notice of termination, and minimum wage rates form the legal floor. An award is a legally binding document setting minimum pay and conditions for a whole industry or occupation, and an enterprise agreement is bargained between one employer and its employees, usually with a union, and must leave employees better off overall than the award. Other employment contracts cover the different ways a person can be engaged: permanent full time, permanent part time, casual, fixed term, or an individual common law contract, which is common for senior staff, while independent contractors work under a contract for service rather than a contract of employment. Work health and safety law requires the employer to provide safe systems of work, training, supervision and protective equipment, and workers compensation is a compulsory employer funded insurance scheme that pays medical costs, income replacement and rehabilitation for a worker injured at work. Antidiscrimination law makes it unlawful to treat a person less favourably because of a protected attribute such as sex, race, age, disability, marital status or religion, and equal employment opportunity requires policies that give all employees equal access to recruitment, training and promotion.
business.hr.key-influences.legal.why: Compliance is not optional because breaches bring fines, compensation orders and tribunal action, while safe, fair and non discriminatory workplaces reduce disputes, absenteeism and turnover and protect the reputation of the business.
business.hr.key-influences.legal.exam: Asked as explain, analyse or assess how the legal framework influences human resource management, usually applied to a case study workplace. Name the specific part of the framework you are using rather than saying the law generally.

business.hr.key-influences.economic.subject: business_studies
business.hr.key-influences.economic.what: Economic influences are conditions in the business cycle, which is the pattern of upswing and downturn in economic activity, and in the labour market, which is the supply of workers with the skills a business needs and the demand for them. In an upswing, businesses recruit, offer overtime and lift pay to attract scarce skills. In a downturn, businesses freeze wages, cut hours, use more casual staff or retrench staff, and retrenchment means ending a job because the business no longer needs that work done. Global competition adds constant pressure on labour costs, being wages plus on costs such as superannuation and workers compensation premiums.
business.hr.key-influences.economic.why: Because wages are a major expense, economic conditions decide whether human resource management is recruiting and training or shrinking and managing separation, which directly affects morale, skill retention and cost control.
business.hr.key-influences.economic.exam: Asked as explain or analyse the impact of economic influences, paired with recruitment, separation and global competition in extended responses.

business.hr.key-influences.technological.subject: business_studies
business.hr.key-influences.technological.what: Technological influences are the ways new equipment, systems and automation change what work is done and how it is done. Technology automates routine tasks, removes some jobs and creates others needing higher skills, and it supports human resource management itself through electronic records, online recruitment, online learning and performance data systems. When technology takes the judgement out of a task and leaves a simple routine, the job is deskilled, and this loss of skill in a role is called deskilling, so the skill level and often the pay of that role fall, while other roles need higher skills. Technology also enables flexible work, meaning employees can vary when and where they work, including working from home.
business.hr.key-influences.technological.why: Technology raises productivity but forces retraining, which is teaching existing employees the new skills the changed job needs, and it can trigger resistance to change, where employees oppose a new system because they fear job loss, closer monitoring or looking unskilled, so managers must consult, communicate the benefits and train before the change.
business.hr.key-influences.technological.exam: Asked as explain or analyse the impact of technology on human resource management, usually linked to training and development and job design.

business.hr.key-influences.social.subject: business_studies
business.hr.key-influences.social.point: social – changing work patterns, living standards
business.hr.key-influences.social.what: Social influences come from change in society. Changing work patterns include flexible hours, working from home, an ageing workforce and greater workforce diversity, meaning employing people of different ages, cultures, genders and abilities. The shift towards a workforce with a higher proportion of casual and contract employees rather than permanent staff is called casualisation, which gives the employer flexibility to match staff to demand but gives the employee less security and no paid leave. Living standards refers to community expectations about pay, conditions, job security and work life balance, meaning the fit between working hours and personal or family life, which rise over time.
business.hr.key-influences.social.why: Businesses that ignore these expectations cannot attract or keep staff, so flexible arrangements and family friendly policies become genuine retention tools that lower absenteeism and strengthen the reputation of the employer.
business.hr.key-influences.social.exam: Asked as describe or explain social influences on human resource management, paired with maintenance strategies and with staff retention.

business.hr.key-influences.ethics-and-co.subject: business_studies
business.hr.key-influences.ethics-and-co.what: Legal compliance means meeting the minimum the law demands, such as paying award rates, meeting work health and safety duties and not discriminating, and it is not optional. Ethical responsibility is voluntary and goes further than the law: paying above the award, offering flexible hours to carers, or auditing overseas contractors when no Australian law requires it. In human resources, ethics covers fair pay, safe conditions, honest recruitment, employee privacy, meaning employee records and monitoring data are kept confidential and used only for proper purposes, and freedom from discrimination and harassment. Corporate social responsibility means the business voluntarily accepting responsibility for the social and environmental impact of its decisions, including their effect on employees.
business.hr.key-influences.ethics-and-co.why: Ethical human resource management builds trust, loyalty and a strong corporate culture and protects reputation, while exposure of unsafe, underpaid or exploitative work damages the brand, customer support and the ability to recruit good staff.
business.hr.key-influences.ethics-and-co.exam: Asked as assess or evaluate ethics and corporate social responsibility, paired with the difference between legal compliance and ethical responsibility. Give one compliance example and one voluntary example to show the contrast.

business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.subject: business_studies
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.what: Acquisition is getting the right number of staff with the right skills. It begins with human resource planning to forecast how many staff and which skills will be needed, then job analysis, which studies the job to produce a job description listing the duties of the job and a job specification listing the skills, qualifications and personal qualities the person needs, then recruitment to attract applicants, then selection using applications, interviews, testing and referee checks to choose the best fit.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.why: Careful acquisition lowers turnover and training costs because a good match between person and job performs sooner, while a poor appointment wastes money, damages team morale and raises the risk of later dismissal disputes.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.exam: Asked as outline or explain acquisition, and required as one of the four processes when a question says discuss the processes of human resource management.

business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.subject: business_studies
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.what: Development is building employee skills and abilities over time. Induction settles new staff into the job, the workplace and the culture. Training builds skills for the current job, using on the job methods such as coaching while doing the actual work, or off the job methods such as courses away from the workplace. Development prepares staff for future roles through mentoring, further study and job rotation, which moves employees between different jobs so they learn a wider range of tasks.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.why: Development raises productivity and quality, keeps the workforce flexible when technology or demand changes, and improves motivation and retention because employees can see a career path inside the business.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.exam: Asked as explain or assess how development contributes to business performance, paired with technological change and with staff turnover.

business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.subject: business_studies
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.what: Maintenance is keeping employees committed, safe and staying with the business. It covers meeting legal responsibilities for pay and working conditions, being hours, breaks, leave and safety arrangements, providing communication systems so information flows both ways, employee participation where staff have a genuine say in decisions affecting their work, benefits and flexible arrangements that support work life balance, and handling grievances so problems are settled early.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.why: Maintenance reduces staff turnover, the proportion of employees who leave and must be replaced, and absenteeism, which saves recruitment and retraining costs and keeps corporate knowledge inside the business, and it lowers disputation because concerns are resolved before they escalate.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.exam: Asked as explain or assess maintenance as a process, paired with the effectiveness indicators of turnover, absenteeism and worker satisfaction.

business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.subject: business_studies
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.what: Separation is the ending of the employment relationship. It is voluntary when the employee chooses to leave, through resignation, voluntary redundancy or retirement, and involuntary when the employer decides, through dismissal for misconduct or poor performance, or through retrenchment, also called forced redundancy, where the job itself is no longer needed. Correct procedures, warnings, notice and final entitlements must be followed in every case.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.why: Managed well, separation controls labour costs and removes poor performers. Managed badly it produces an unfair dismissal claim, where a former employee argues to a tribunal that the dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable, along with low morale among the staff who remain and lasting damage to the reputation of the employer.
business.hr.processes-of-human-resource-.exam: Asked as distinguish between voluntary and involuntary separation, or explain how separation is managed legally and ethically in a case study.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: leadership style
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Leadership style is how a manager directs, motivates and communicates with staff. An autocratic style makes decisions alone and gives instructions to be followed, which suits crises, safety critical tasks and routine standardised work. A participative or democratic style consults employees and shares decision making. The style chosen shapes communication flows, employee participation and corporate culture, which is the shared values, beliefs and behaviour of the people in the business.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Style drives motivation, initiative and disputation, because participative leadership usually lifts commitment and retention, while autocratic leadership gives speed and control but can raise conflict, absenteeism and turnover.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as assess or evaluate the effectiveness of a leadership style, paired with corporate culture, motivation and levels of disputation.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: job design – general or specific tasks
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Job design decides the tasks and responsibilities that make up a job. Specific job design builds a job from specific tasks: narrow, repetitive, specialised work that is learned quickly and done efficiently. General job design builds a job from general tasks: a broad role created through multiskilling, meaning training employees to perform several different tasks, together with job rotation, job enlargement, which adds more tasks at the same level, job enrichment, which adds responsibility and decision making, and teamwork.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Specific design suits standardised low cost production but causes boredom, absenteeism and turnover, while general design lifts motivation and flexibility, although it demands more training and can raise labour costs.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as compare, assess or evaluate general and specific job design, paired with motivation, cost leadership and workforce flexibility. Use the syllabus words general and specific rather than only saying specialisation.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: recruitment – internal or external, general or specific skills
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Recruitment attracts suitable applicants for a job. Internal recruitment fills the job by promoting or transferring an existing employee. External recruitment draws people from outside the business using advertising, online job sites, recruitment agencies, universities and referrals. The business also chooses between hiring general skills, which are transferable and can be trained further, and specific skills, which are ready to use in that job immediately.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Internal recruitment is cheaper, faster and motivating because staff see a career path, but it can recycle old thinking, while external recruitment brings fresh skills and ideas at higher cost and with greater risk that the person will not fit the culture.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: training and development – current or future skills
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Training builds the skills an employee needs for the job right now, such as induction, a new software system or a new machine, and is usually short and specific. Much of it is on the job training, meaning learning while doing the actual work under supervision. Development builds broader capability for future roles and future business needs, through mentoring, where an experienced employee guides a less experienced one, plus job rotation, leadership programs and further education, so it is longer term.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Training only for current skills keeps costs low but leaves the business exposed when technology or markets shift, while investing in future skills creates a flexible workforce and a promotion pool that improves retention.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as analyse or evaluate training and development strategies, paired with technological change and with the effectiveness indicators.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: performance management – developmental or administrative
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Performance management measures and improves employee performance against agreed standards. An appraisal is a formal review of an employee's performance, and methods include self appraisal, where the employee rates their own work, 360 degree feedback, which gathers views from the manager, peers, subordinates and sometimes customers, and management by objectives, where the employee and manager agree measurable goals in advance and performance is judged against whether those goals were met. A developmental purpose uses the results to coach, set goals and identify training needs. An administrative purpose uses the same results to decide pay, promotion, transfer, demotion or dismissal.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: A developmental focus raises skills, motivation and honest feedback, but when employees see appraisal only as an administrative judgement tied to pay or dismissal, honesty falls, stress rises and disputation can increase.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as distinguish between developmental and administrative purposes, or assess performance management, paired with rewards and with motivation.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: rewards – monetary and non-monetary, individual or group, performance pay
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Rewards are what employees receive in return for their work. Monetary rewards are payments and include wages, salaries, bonuses, share plans and superannuation above the legal minimum. Non monetary rewards are valued benefits that are not cash, such as flexible hours, extra leave, recognition, training and a company car. Individual rewards go to one employee and suit work with measurable individual output, while group rewards go to a whole team or the whole workforce and suit work that depends on cooperation. Performance pay links payment directly to measured results such as sales or targets met.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Well designed rewards attract, motivate and retain staff and point effort at business objectives, although individual performance pay can damage teamwork and encourage short term or unethical behaviour when the measures are poorly chosen.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as evaluate or assess rewards as a human resource strategy, paired with motivation, retention and performance management.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: global – costs, skills, supply
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Global human resource strategy staffs a business operating across countries. Costs means comparing wage levels and on costs between nations and deciding where work is done. Skills means choosing between local employees, expatriates, who are employees sent from the home country, and third country nationals, and training staff to work across cultural difference, such as different expectations about authority, teamwork and working hours. Supply means locating operations where enough qualified labour is available.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Global strategies can cut labour costs and reach scarce skills, but they raise cultural difference, different employment laws in each country, questions about the ethical treatment of overseas workers, and the high cost and failure rate of expatriate placements.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as assess or evaluate global human resource strategies, paired with outsourcing to global contractors and with ethics and corporate social responsibility.

business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.subject: business_studies
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.point: workplace disputes
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.what: Workplace disputes are disagreements between employers and employees over pay, conditions, safety or management decisions. They show up as industrial action, meaning strikes, work bans or lockouts, and as absenteeism or formal grievances. Resolution methods are negotiation, where the parties bargain directly to reach agreement, mediation, where a neutral third party helps them reach their own agreement without imposing one, grievance procedures, being a set internal process for raising a complaint and having it dealt with at rising levels of management, and involvement of courts and tribunals, which hear the matter and can impose a binding decision.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.why: Disputes cost output, wages and customer goodwill, so settling them early through negotiation or grievance procedures is cheaper and preserves the working relationship, while courts and tribunals are slow, costly and impose an outcome neither side controls.
business.hr.strategies-in-human-resource.exam: Asked as explain, compare or evaluate methods of resolving workplace disputes, usually with stimulus describing a dispute needing the best method.

business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.subject: business_studies
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.what: Indicators show whether human resource management is working. Corporate culture is the shared values and behaviour of staff. Benchmarking key variables compares the results of the business against best practice, industry standards or its own other sites. Changes in staff turnover show whether people are staying. Absenteeism counts unplanned days off. Accidents measure safety performance. Levels of disputation count grievances, and time lost to industrial action. Worker satisfaction is gathered through surveys, exit interviews and observation.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.why: Indicators turn human resource management into measurable evidence, so rising turnover, absenteeism, accidents or disputes signal problems in leadership, job design or maintenance and let managers act before productivity and costs suffer.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.exam: Asked as assess or evaluate the effectiveness of human resource management, where extended responses apply several indicators to a chosen business.

business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.subject: business_studies
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.point: 120 indicative hours are required to complete the course.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.what: The requirement appears twice because both courses carry 120 indicative hours: 120 for the Preliminary course studied in Year 11 and 120 for the HSC course, which is 240 indicative hours across the two years. Indicative hours are the time NESA expects teaching and learning of the course to take. The HSC 120 hours are divided across the four HSC topics, being Operations, Marketing, Finance and Human resources.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.why: Knowing that each course carries its own 120 hours explains why Preliminary content is treated as assumed knowledge rather than taught again, and why no HSC topic can be left until the end of the course.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.exam: Not examined as content. It sets the size of each course and explains how teaching and revision time is divided across the four HSC topics.

business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.subject: business_studies
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.point: the Preliminary course is a prerequisite
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.what: A course requirement: the Preliminary course is a prerequisite, meaning students must complete Preliminary Business Studies before starting the HSC course. The Preliminary course covers nature of business, business management and business planning, which supply foundation ideas such as stakeholders, management roles, the key business functions and the business life cycle that the HSC course assumes you already know.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.why: HSC Human resources builds directly on that foundation, so gaps in Preliminary understanding of stakeholders and the key business functions make interdependence, influences and strategies much harder to explain accurately.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.exam: Not examined directly. Preliminary concepts are assumed knowledge that supports HSC answers rather than being tested as separate questions.

business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.subject: business_studies
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.point: suggested components and weightings for the internal assessment of the Preliminary course
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.what: A course requirement describing internal assessment, which is the marking schools do themselves during the Preliminary course. The suggested components cover knowledge and understanding of course content, stimulus based skills, inquiry and research, and communication of business information, ideas and issues in appropriate forms, each carrying a weighting that NESA suggests rather than mandates.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.why: These components show what is actually valued: not only recalling content, but interpreting stimulus material, researching real businesses and communicating findings in report and extended response form.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.exam: Not an exam topic. It shapes Preliminary assessment tasks, which practise the same skills the external HSC examination later tests.

business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.subject: business_studies
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.point: mandatory components and weightings for the internal assessment of the HSC course
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.what: A course requirement: the internal assessment schools run during the HSC course must use mandatory components, being knowledge and understanding of course content, stimulus based skills, inquiry and research, and communication of business information, ideas and issues in appropriate forms, each with a weighting that NESA sets rather than suggests.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.why: Because these components are mandatory, school assessment mirrors the examination, so practising stimulus interpretation, case study research and structured extended writing lifts both the internal mark and the final HSC result.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.exam: Not examined as content. It explains why assessment tasks combine case study research, stimulus response questions and extended writing.

business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.subject: business_studies
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.point: the HSC examination specifications, which describe the format of the external HSC examination.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.what: A course requirement: the examination specifications set out the format of the paper. The Business Studies HSC examination is written, draws on all four HSC topics, and uses multiple choice questions, short answer questions, a business report based on stimulus material, and extended response questions requiring sustained argument about business situations.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.why: Knowing the format lets you prepare deliberately, because memorised content alone earns little: marks come from applying content to stimulus and structuring extended responses using correct business terminology.
business.hr.effectiveness-of-human-resou.exam: Not content itself. It describes the paper, including the business report and extended response sections where Human resources is frequently assessed.
